news.content_title: National flu and COVID-19 surveillance report: 19 November 2026 (week 47)
news.content: This publication is licensed under the terms of the Open Government Licence v3.0 except where otherwise stated. To view this licence, visit nationalarchives.gov.uk/doc/open-government-licence/version/3 or write to the Information Policy Team, The National Archives, Kew, London TW9 4DU, or email: psi@nationalarchives.gov.uk . Where we have identified any third party copyright information you will need to obtain permission from the copyright holders concerned. This publication is available at https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/national-flu-and-covid-19-surveillance-reports-2026-to-2027-season/national-flu-and-covid-19-surveillance-report-19-november-2026-week-47 This report summarises the information from the surveillance systems which are used to monitor COVID-19 (caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2)), influenza, respiratory syncytial virus ( RSV ) and diseases caused by other seasonal respiratory viruses in England. The report is based on data up to week 46 of 2026 (9 November to 15 November 2026). The main messages of this report are: Annual reports for the 2025 to 2026 season: Influenza in the UK, annual epidemiological report: winter 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Epidemiology of COVID-19 in England (published 25 June 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in all GP patients: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in school-aged children: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in frontline healthcare workers: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Influenza activity increased and is circulating at low levels. Emergency department ( ED ) attendances for influenza-like-illness ( ILI ) increased and were above seasonally expected levels. The number of influenza-confirmed acute respiratory infection ( ARI ) incidents increased compared with the previous week. A briefing note has been issued to inform the NHS that influenza activity is now above baseline levels. Compared with the equivalent week last season (week 46 data, 2025 to 2026), vaccine uptake is lower among patients aged 65 years and over (65.8% vs 67.8%), patients aged 6 months to under 65 years in clinical risk groups (32.5% vs 33.5%), those aged 2 years (37.6% vs 38.5%), and those aged 3 years (37.5% vs 38.8%). In contrast, vaccine uptake is higher among pregnant women (33.9% vs 32.8%). COVID-19 activity was stable and is circulating at low levels. ED attendances for COVID-19-like illness decreased. The number of COVID-19 confirmed acute respiratory infections ( ARI ) incidents increased compared with the previous week. By the end of week 46 2026, 54.5% of all people aged 75 years and over in England had been vaccinated with an autumn 2026 dose. Similarly, 23.1% of all people aged under 75 years with a weakened immune system in England had been vaccinated with an autumn 2026 dose since 1 October 2026. RSV activity increased and is circulating at low levels. ED attendances for acute bronchiolitis increased and were below seasonally expected levels. Note 1: these indicators use the moving epidemic method ( MEM ) and the mean standard deviation method ( MSD ) to define thresholds to determine their respective levels of activity. Further information on these methods can be found in Influenza surveillance in Europe: establishing epidemic thresholds by the Moving Epidemic Method and Setting thresholds to determine COVID-19 activity levels using the mean standard deviation ( MSD ) method, England, 2022 to 2024 . The MEM approach is well-established for some influenza surveillance indicators, however, for other indicators both the MEM and MSD are experimental and may be subject to future revision. Influenza laboratory surveillance and GP swabbing positivity have transitioned from using MEM to using MSD . These approaches will be considered alongside expert opinion and triangulation of other data sources. The Second Generation Surveillance System ( SGSS ) captures test result information for notifiable infectious diseases, including COVID-19 and influenza, from laboratories in England. The unified sample dataset ( USD ) stores all SARS-CoV-2 test results reported to SGSS , Respiratory DataMart and UKHSA laboratories, and is used to calculate the percentage of tests positive for SARS-CoV-2 among all SARS-CoV-2 tests conducted. As of 17 November 2026, there were a total of 1,826 COVID-19 cases identified in hospital settings in week 46, remaining stable compared with 1,792 cases in the previous week. SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) PCR positivity in hospital settings remained stable in week 46, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 7.0% up to Sunday 15 November 2026 compared with 7.2% for the same period on the previous Sunday. Positivity rates were highest among those aged 85 years and over with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 9.9% up to Sunday 15 November 2026. This has remained stable compared with 10.4% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. Note 2: data from previous seasons is aligned by day. Note 3: testing policy and practice may change over time which can impact positivity rates, therefore comparisons over time should be interpreted with caution. Notable changes in testing policy occurred during 2022 to 2023, which are outlined in the data quality report . Note 4: the highlighted line corresponds to the age group in the subplot title, grey lines correspond to all other age groups. Influenza positivity increased in week 46, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 11.4% up to Sunday 15 November 2026. This is compared with 8.3% on the previous Sunday. By type, influenza A positivity increased in week 46, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 10.1% up to Sunday 15 November 2026. Influenza B positivity remained stable in the same week, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 0.3% up to Sunday 15 November 2026. Influenza A positivity rates were highest among those aged between 5 and 11 years, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 23.2% up to Sunday 15 November 2026. This has increased from 13.3% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. Influenza B positivity rates for the same period were highest among those aged between 12 and 17 years, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 2.1%. This has increased from 1.4% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. RSV swab-positivity-based PCR test results reported through SGSS have been included as a pilot indicator from week 49 2025 onwards. RSV positivity increased in week 46, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 5.1% up to Sunday 15 November 2026, compared with 3.2% up to the previous Sunday. RSV positivity rates were highest in those aged between 0 and 4 years with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 28.8% up to Sunday 15 November 2026 in week 46. This has increased from 19.1% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. Respiratory DataMart is a sentinel laboratory-based surveillance system where participating laboratories report positive and negative test results for a number of respiratory viruses from samples primarily taken in hospital. A small proportion of primary care samples are also included in this reporting. In week 46, data is based on reporting from 9 out of the 14 sentinel laboratories. In week 46, 5,156 respiratory specimens reported through the Respiratory DataMart System were tested for influenza. There were 588 positive samples for influenza: 397 influenza A (not subtyped), 7 influenza A (H3N2), 166 influenza A (H1N1)pdm09, and 20 influenza B. Overall, influenza positivity increased to 11.4% in week 46 compared with 8.0% in the previous week. In week 46, 5,437 respiratory specimens reported through the Respiratory DataMart System were tested for SARS-CoV-2. There were 346 positive samples for SARS-CoV-2. SARS-CoV-2 positivity increased slightly to 6.4% compared with 6.0% in the previous week, with the highest positivity in those aged 80 years and over at 9.3%. RSV positivity increased to 5.2%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 26.7%. Adenovirus positivity decreased slightly to 1.6%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 5.1%. Human metapneumovirus ( hMPV ) positivity increased to 0.7%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 1.7%. Parainfluenza positivity decreased slightly to 2.9%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 8.7%. Rhinovirus positivity decreased to 11.3%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 28.5%. DataMart data is provisional and subject to retrospective updates. Note 5: shading represents 95% confidence intervals. UKHSA conducts genomic surveillance of SARS-CoV-2 lineages. This section provides an overview of circulating lineages in England, derived from data on sequenced PCR -positive SARS-CoV-2 samples in SGSS . The prevalence of UKHSA -designated lineages among sequenced cases is presented in Figure 13. To account for reporting delays, we report the proportion of lineages within COVID-19 cases that have had a sequenced positive sample between 12 October 2026 and 25 October 2026. Note that low sequencing numbers, especially within the latest reporting period, will impact the accuracy of the prevalence estimates. These most recent figures should therefore be interpreted with caution. Note that lineages will be grouped independently from their parent lineage once they reach sufficient prevalence, and may be re-grouped into their parent lineage if their prevalence subsequently falls. The data quality report contains more information on lineage groupings. Analysis of viruses from primary and secondary care shows that circulating A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses show low genetic diversity and all belong to clade D.3.1.1. Observations published from the World Health Organization (WHO) influenza vaccine composition meeting (VCM) in September 2026 suggest low reactivity of some viruses within the D.3.1.1 subclade with post-infection ferret antisera raised against A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like virus – the A(H1N1)pdm09 component in 2026 Southern and 2026/2027 Northern Hemisphere cell- and egg-based influenza vaccines - and human sera post-vaccination with the Southern Hemisphere vaccine 2026. It is not yet clear how vaccine effectiveness against clinical disease may be affected by these observations. Vaccines typically still provide protection against severe clinical disease when drifted strains are seen with only a modest reduction in effectiveness. The characterisation of circulating A(H3N2) viruses shows that A(H3N2) viruses are currently showing low genetic diversity. All sequenced viruses to date belong to genetic subclade K. To date, only a small number of influenza B viruses have been detected, which show some genetic diversity. Between week 35 2026 (week ending 30 August 2026) and week 46 2026 (week ending 15 November 2026), the UKHSA respiratory virus unit ( RVU ) has genetically characterised 477 seasonal influenza viruses, and identified 343 influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses, 100 influenza A(H3N2) viruses, and 34 influenza B viruses. Details of the characterised viruses by subtype are shown in Tables 1, 2 and 3. The RVU has confirmed by genome sequencing the detection of live attenuated influenza vaccine ( LAIV ) viruses in 17 influenza A/B positive samples, collected from children aged between 2 and 16 years. UKHSA RVU performs antigenic characterisation of influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, influenza A(H3N2) and influenza B viruses using haemagglutination inhibition ( HI ) assays. Data from these assays are used to compare how similar the currently circulating influenza viruses are to the strains included in seasonal influenza vaccines, and to monitor for changes in circulating influenza viruses. Similarity of currently circulating influenza strains to vaccine strains is defined as having an antibody titre within 4-fold when compared with reference viruses representative of the vaccine strain. Antigenic characterisation of viruses in the current reporting period is underway. A(H1N1)pdm09: 13 A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses have been antigenically characterised and 11 were similar to reference viruses representative of the A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like Northern Hemisphere 2026/27 (H1N1)pdm09 vaccine strains. A(H3N2): 6 A(H3N2) viruses have been antigenically characterised and 6 were similar to reference viruses representative of the A/Darwin/1454/2025 (H3N2)-like and A/Darwin/1415/2025 (H3N2)-like Northern Hemisphere 2026/27 (H3N2) vaccine strains. Influenza positive samples are screened for mutations in the virus neuraminidase ( NA ) and the cap-dependent endonuclease of the polymerase acidic protein (PA) genes known to confer neuraminidase inhibitor (oseltamivir and zanamivir) or baloxavir resistance, respectively. Results from this surveillance are given in Table 4. There have been 9 detections with mutations related to reduced susceptibility/resistance to oseltamivir and/or reduced susceptibility to baloxavir. Data is presented on viral ARI incidents in different settings that are reported to UKHSA health protection teams ( HPTs ). Please note that reporting practices are known to vary between seasons and between regions. Any interpretation of temporal and regional trends should consider the likelihood of differences in reporting of ARI incidents over time and between regions. There were 147 new ARI incidents reported in week 46 in England. These included: 119 incidents from care homes, of which 26 were due to influenza A, 17 were due to SARS-CoV-2, 17 were due to influenza (no type information available), 7 were due to multiple pathogens, 5 were due to other pathogens and 3 were due to RSV . No pathogen was reported in 44 incidents 1 incident from hospitals, of which 1 was due to SARS-CoV-2 21 incidents from educational settings, of which 6 were due to influenza A, 5 were due to RSV and 1 was due to influenza (no type information available). No pathogen was reported in 9 incidents 1 incident from prisons, of which 1 was due to influenza A 5 incidents from other settings, of which 3 were due to SARS-CoV-2 and 1 was due to influenza (no type information available). No pathogen was reported in 1 incident FluSurvey is an internet-based participatory surveillance system based on the InfluenzaNet platform. It monitors trends of influenza-like illness ( ILI ) in the community using self-reported respiratory symptoms from registered participants. As a participatory surveillance system, new signups can occur throughout the season and participation can vary in each week. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control ( ECDC ) ILI case definition of sudden onset of symptoms with at least one of fever (chills), malaise, headache, muscle pain and at least one of cough, sore throat, shortness of breath is used for reporting. Please note that ILI is a broad definition and can include other respiratory illnesses such as COVID-19. Healthcare use is presented as self-reported use of health services among participants meeting the ILI ECDC case definition. Where a person reports use of more than one health care service, secondary care will be indicated over primary care use and physical attendance to primary care will be indicated over use of remote services (for example, online NHS services, telephoning their GP or 111). During week commencing 9 November 2026: there were 2,522 participants who completed the weekly symptoms questionnaire 396 (15.7%) reported fever or cough and 129 (5.1%) met the ILI case definition, in the past week 15.5% of participants meeting the ILI case definition reported contact with healthcare services as a result of self-reported symptoms; the most frequently reported contact was a visit to the GP the proportion of participants meeting the ILI case definition remained stable compared with the previous report week (5.1% compared with 5.1% in week 45) data submitted in the current week (commencing 16 November) is available on the UKHSA data dashboard to support more timely insights. For further details see the data quality report Syndromic surveillance collects data from various healthcare sources where presentations are classified by patterns of symptoms compatible with specific infections. In some settings, the syndromic diagnosis can be supplemented by (rapid) testing. In this report, ED attendances are displayed. Further details and data from other syndromic surveillance systems can be found in the syndromic surveillance weekly summaries . During the week ending on 15 November 2026, ED attendances for acute respiratory infections increased and were similar to the seasonally expected level. ED attendances for COVID-19-like illness increased. ED attendances for influenza-like illness increased and were above seasonally expected levels. ED attendances for acute bronchiolitis (a syndrome related to RSV infection) increased and were below seasonally expected levels. NHS 111 triaged calls and online assessments for acute respiratory infections increased in children under the age of 15 years, and remained at seasonally expected levels. GP in-hours consultation rates for upper and lower respiratory tract infections increased, notably in children aged 1 to 4 and 5 to 14 years but remained at seasonally expected levels. Consultation rates for influenza-like illness also increased and are above expected levels. GP out-of-hours daily contacts for respiratory conditions increased, including acute respiratory infections, influenza-like illness and acute bronchitis/bronchiolitis. Contacts for acute respiratory infections and acute bronchitis/bronchiolitis remained at or below baseline levels, while influenza-like illness was above expected levels. Note 6: 7-day moving average is adjusted for bank holidays. Grey columns show weekends and bank holidays. Note 7: the coloured line is the 7-day moving average by age group. Grey lines show the other age groups. The y-axis…

A small proportion of primary care samples are also included in this reporting. In week 46, data is based on reporting from 9 out of the 14 sentinel laboratories. In week 46, 5,156 respiratory specimens reported through the Respiratory DataMart System were tested for influenza. There were 588 positive samples for influenza: 397 influenza A (not subtyped), 7 influenza A (H3N2), 166 influenza A (H1N1)pdm09, and 20 influenza B. Overall, influenza positivity increased to 11.4% in week 46 compared with 8.0% in the previous week. In week 46, 5,437 respiratory specimens reported through the Respiratory DataMart System were tested for SARS-CoV-2. There were 346 positive samples for SARS-CoV-2. SARS-CoV-2 positivity increased slightly to 6.4% compared with 6.0% in the previous week, with the highest positivity in those aged 80 years and over at 9.3%. RSV positivity increased to 5.2%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 26.7%. Adenovirus positivity decreased slightly to 1.6%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 5.1%. Human metapneumovirus ( hMPV ) positivity increased to 0.7%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 1.7%. Parainfluenza positivity decreased slightly to 2.9%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 8.7%. Rhinovirus positivity decreased to 11.3%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 28.5%. DataMart data is provisional and subject to retrospective updates. Note 5: shading represents 95% confidence intervals. UKHSA conducts genomic surveillance of SARS-CoV-2 lineages. This section provides an overview of circulating lineages in England, derived from data on sequenced PCR -positive SARS-CoV-2 samples in SGSS . The prevalence of UKHSA -designated lineages among sequenced cases is presented in Figure 13. To account for reporting delays, we report the proportion of lineages within COVID-19 cases that have had a sequenced positive sample between 12 October 2026 and 25 October 2026. Note that low sequencing numbers, especially within the latest reporting period, will impact the accuracy of the prevalence estimates. These most recent figures should therefore be interpreted with caution. Note that lineages will be grouped independently from their parent lineage once they reach sufficient prevalence, and may be re-grouped into their parent lineage if their prevalence subsequently falls. The data quality report contains more information on lineage groupings. Analysis of viruses from primary and secondary care shows that circulating A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses show low genetic diversity and all belong to clade D.3.1.1. Observations published from the World Health Organization (WHO) influenza vaccine composition meeting (VCM) in September 2026 suggest low reactivity of some viruses within the D.3.1.1 subclade with post-infection ferret antisera raised against A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like virus – the A(H1N1)pdm09 component in 2026 Southern and 2026/2027 Northern Hemisphere cell- and egg-based influenza vaccines - and human sera post-vaccination with the Southern Hemisphere vaccine 2026. It is not yet clear how vaccine effectiveness against clinical disease may be affected by these observations. Vaccines typically still provide protection against severe clinical disease when drifted strains are seen with only a modest reduction in effectiveness. The characterisation of circulating A(H3N2) viruses shows that A(H3N2) viruses are currently showing low genetic diversity. All sequenced viruses to date belong to genetic subclade K. To date, only a small number of influenza B viruses have been detected, which show some genetic diversity. Between week 35 2026 (week ending 30 August 2026) and week 46 2026 (week ending 15 November 2026), the UKHSA respiratory virus unit ( RVU ) has genetically characterised 477 seasonal influenza viruses, and identified 343 influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses, 100 influenza A(H3N2) viruses, and 34 influenza B viruses. Details of the characterised viruses by subtype are shown in Tables 1, 2 and 3. The RVU has confirmed by genome sequencing the detection of live attenuated influenza vaccine ( LAIV ) viruses in 17 influenza A/B positive samples, collected from children aged between 2 and 16 years. UKHSA RVU performs antigenic characterisation of influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, influenza A(H3N2) and influenza B viruses using haemagglutination inhibition ( HI ) assays. Data from these assays are used to compare how similar the currently circulating influenza viruses are to the strains included in seasonal influenza vaccines, and to monitor for changes in circulating influenza viruses. Similarity of currently circulating influenza strains to vaccine strains is defined as having an antibody titre within 4-fold when compared with reference viruses representative of the vaccine strain. Antigenic characterisation of viruses in the current reporting period is underway. A(H1N1)pdm09: 13 A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses have been antigenically characterised and 11 were similar to reference viruses representative of the A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like Northern Hemisphere 2026/27 (H1N1)pdm09 vaccine strains. A(H3N2): 6 A(H3N2) viruses have been antigenically characterised and 6 were similar to reference viruses representative of the A/Darwin/1454/2025 (H3N2)-like and A/Darwin/1415/2025 (H3N2)-like Northern Hemisphere 2026/27 (H3N2) vaccine strains. Influenza positive samples are screened for mutations in the virus neuraminidase ( NA ) and the cap-dependent endonuclease of the polymerase acidic protein (PA) genes known to confer neuraminidase inhibitor (oseltamivir and zanamivir) or baloxavir resistance, respectively. Results from this surveillance are given in Table 4. There have been 9 detections with mutations related to reduced susceptibility/resistance to oseltamivir and/or reduced susceptibility to baloxavir. Data is presented on viral ARI incidents in different settings that are reported to UKHSA health protection teams ( HPTs ). Please note that reporting practices are known to vary between seasons and between regions. Any interpretation of temporal and regional trends should consider the likelihood of differences in reporting of ARI incidents over time and between regions. There were 147 new ARI incidents reported in week 46 in England. These included: 119 incidents from care homes, of which 26 were due to influenza A, 17 were due to SARS-CoV-2, 17 were due to influenza (no type information available), 7 were due to multiple pathogens, 5 were due to other pathogens and 3 were due to RSV . No pathogen was reported in 44 incidents 1 incident from hospitals, of which 1 was due to SARS-CoV-2 21 incidents from educational settings, of which 6 were due to influenza A, 5 were due to RSV and 1 was due to influenza (no type information available). No pathogen was reported in 9 incidents 1 incident from prisons, of which 1 was due to influenza A 5 incidents from other settings, of which 3 were due to SARS-CoV-2 and 1 was due to influenza (no type information available). No pathogen was reported in 1 incident FluSurvey is an internet-based participatory surveillance system based on the InfluenzaNet platform. It monitors trends of influenza-like illness ( ILI ) in the community using self-reported respiratory symptoms from registered participants. As a participatory surveillance system, new signups can occur throughout the season and participation can vary in each week. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control ( ECDC ) ILI case definition of sudden onset of symptoms with at least one of fever (chills), malaise, headache, muscle pain and at least one of cough, sore throat, shortness of breath is used for reporting. Please note that ILI is a broad definition and can include other respiratory illnesses such as COVID-19. Healthcare use is presented as self-reported use of health services among participants meeting the ILI ECDC case definition. Where a person reports use of more than one health care service, secondary care will be indicated over primary care use and physical attendance to primary care will be indicated over use of remote services (for example, online NHS services, telephoning their GP or 111). During week commencing 9 November 2026: there were 2,522 participants who completed the weekly symptoms questionnaire 396 (15.7%) reported fever or cough and 129 (5.1%) met the ILI case definition, in the past week 15.5% of participants meeting the ILI case definition reported contact with healthcare services as a result of self-reported symptoms; the most frequently reported contact was a visit to the GP the proportion of participants meeting the ILI case definition remained stable compared with the previous report week (5.1% compared with 5.1% in week 45) data submitted in the current week (commencing 16 November) is available on the UKHSA data dashboard to support more timely insights. For further details see the data quality report Syndromic surveillance collects data from various healthcare sources where presentations are classified by patterns of symptoms compatible with specific infections. In some settings, the syndromic diagnosis can be supplemented by (rapid) testing. In this report, ED attendances are displayed. Further details and data from other syndromic surveillance systems can be found in the syndromic surveillance weekly summaries . During the week ending on 15 November 2026, ED attendances for acute respiratory infections increased and were similar to the seasonally expected level. ED attendances for COVID-19-like illness increased. ED attendances for influenza-like illness increased and were above seasonally expected levels. ED attendances for acute bronchiolitis (a syndrome related to RSV infection) increased and were below seasonally expected levels. NHS 111 triaged calls and online assessments for acute respiratory infections increased in children under the age of 15 years, and remained at seasonally expected levels. GP in-hours consultation rates for upper and lower respiratory tract infections increased, notably in children aged 1 to 4 and 5 to 14 years but remained at seasonally expected levels. Consultation rates for influenza-like illness also increased and are above expected levels. GP out-of-hours daily contacts for respiratory conditions increased, including acute respiratory infections, influenza-like illness and acute bronchitis/bronchiolitis. Contacts for acute respiratory infections and acute bronchitis/bronchiolitis remained at or below baseline levels, while influenza-like illness was above expected levels. news.title_original: National flu and COVID-19 surveillance report: 19 November 2026 (week 47) - GOV.UK

analysis.time: The report was published on 19 November 2026, and the data it references covers up to week 46 of 2026 (9 November to 15 November 2026).
analysis.location_and_population: The report focuses on England, with specific mention of populations aged 75 years and over, those under 75 with weakened immune systems, and age groups such as 85 years and over.
analysis.event: The report details the surveillance findings for SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19), influenza, and RSV in England during week 46 of 2026. It notes that SARS-CoV-2 activity remained stable, influenza activity increased, and RSV activity also increased.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: As of 17 November 2026, there were 1,826 confirmed SARS-CoV-2 cases in hospital settings during week 46. Influenza positivity increased to 11.4% compared to 8.3% in the previous week, with influenza A positivity at 10.1% and influenza B at 0.3%. RSV activity increased, with acute bronchiolitis ED attendances rising.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The report indicates that influenza activity is above baseline levels, and a briefing note has been issued to the NHS. The data is based on surveillance systems and is subject to retrospective updates. The methods used (MEM and MSD) are experimental and may be revised, and comparisons over time should be interpreted with caution due to potential changes in testing policy.

analysis.brief_en: The National Flu and COVID-19 Surveillance Report for 19 November 2026 (week 47) provides an overview of the health situation in England. It notes that SARS-CoV-2 activity remained stable, with 1,826 confirmed cases in hospital settings during week 46. Influenza activity increased, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 11.4% compared to 8.3% in the previous week. Influenza A positivity rose to 10.1%, while influenza B remained stable at 0.3%. RSV activity also increased, with ED attendances for acute bronchiolitis rising. The report highlights that influenza is circulating above baseline levels and that a briefing note has been issued to the NHS. The data is based on surveillance systems and is subject to retrospective updates. The methods used to determine activity levels, such as the Moving Epidemic Method (MEM) and Mean Standard Deviation (MSD), are experimental and may be revised. Testing policies have changed over time, which could affect positivity rates, so comparisons should be made cautiously. The report was published on 19 November 2026, with data up to 15 November 2026.

news.source_body_en: The National Flu and COVID-19 Surveillance Report for 19 November 2026 (week 47) provides an overview of the health situation in England. It notes that SARS-CoV-2 activity remained stable, with 1,826 confirmed cases in hospital settings during week 46. news.content_zh: 2026 年 11 月 19 日(第 47 周)的国家流感和 新型冠状病毒感染 监测 报告概述了英格兰的健康状况。报告指出,严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2 活动保持稳定,第 46 周期间医院环境中有 1,826 例确诊病例。流感活动增加,滚动 7 天阳性率为 11.4%,而前一周为 8.3%。甲型流感阳性率升至10.1%,乙型流感阳性率稳定在0.3%。RSV 活动也增加,急性细支气管炎急诊就诊人数增加。该报告强调,流感的传播程度高于基线水平,并且已向国民医疗服务体系(NHS)发出了一份简报。该数据基于监测系统,并会进行回顾性更新。用于确定活动水平的方法,例如移动流行病方法 (MEM) 和平均标准差 (MSD),是实验性的,可能会进行修订。检测政策随着时间的推移而发生变化,这可能会影响阳性率,因此应谨慎进行比较。该报告于2026年11月19日发布,数据截至2026年11月15日。

Careers Internships & Fellowships Apprenticeships & Workforce Development Work at DOE Funding Opportunities Breadcrumb Biological and Environmental Research Redesigned Hepatitis C Drug Becomes a Powerful New Treatment for COVID-19 Redesigned Hepatitis C Drug Becomes a Powerful New Treatment for COVID-19 Scientists transformed an old drug into a potent COVID-19 treatment effective against drug-resistant variants. Biological and Environmental Research February 19, 2026 Estimated Read Time 3 min The final version of the redesigned drug binds tightly to the main COVID-19 protease, an enzyme the virus needs to multiply. The drug’s structure is effective even against mutated forms that resist other treatments. Image courtesy of Stanford University The Science Researchers have redesigned the hepatitis C drug boceprevir to create a more effective treatment for COVID-19. Some virus variants no longer respond well to current therapies, like Paxlovid, due to mutations in the main COVID-19 virus protease (Mpro). This is a key enzyme the virus uses to replicate. Mpro is essential to the virus and remains intact from variant to variant. As such, it is an ideal target for treatments to focus on. Using X-ray crystal structures, scientists refined boceprevir atom by atom. They worked to improve how the drug binds within key pockets of the enzyme. The researchers used the Stanford Synchrotron Radiation Lightsource (a DOE Office of Science User Facility) to analyze the crystal structure when the drug was attached to Mpro. The Impact This research produced a drug that is effective against COVID-19 strains that are resistant to existing treatments. The resulting compound, ML2006a4, binds more tightly and durably than earlier drugs. It also shows superior protection in preclinical animal studies. By redesigning an older hepatitis C drug, scientists made it more effective against mutated forms of the virus’s protease. This could help doctors treat patients who no longer respond to existing therapies. Summary Boceprevir is a protease inhibitor originally developed to treat hepatitis C. Scientists adapted this drug to target the main protease (Mpro) of SARS-CoV-2. This is a critical enzyme the virus uses to process its polyproteins and replicate. Because Mpro is conserved across variants and has no close human equivalent, it remains a prime target for antiviral drug development. However, some SARS-CoV-2 variants contain mutations in Mpro that reduce the effectiveness of existing treatments. Using X-ray crystallography data collected at the Macromolecular Crystallography Beamlines at the Stanford Synchrotron Radiation Lightsource (SSRL), researchers determined high-resolution structures of Mpro bound to various boceprevir analogs. These structural insights guided a stepwise redesign of the molecule to improve its fit within the enzyme’s active site and sub-pockets. The team optimized interactions and reduced internal strains within the drug’s structure to improve binding, potency, and resistance profile. The final compound, ML2006a4, binds covalently to Mpro and retains strong activity even against variants harboring resistance-associated mutations. This structure-guided approach demonstrates how iterative design can yield next-generation antivirals with broad-spectrum activity. It also underscores the vital role of DOE- and NIH-supported synchrotron-based methods in accelerating drug discovery against emerging viral threats. Contact Michael Lin Stanford University mzlin@stanford.edu Funding Funding for this research included: Sarafan ChEM-H and the Innovative Medicines Accelerator, Harrington Scholar-Innovator Award, Emergent Ventures at the Mercatus Center at George Mason University, Stanford-Coulter Translational Research Grant, National Institute of Health(NIH)/National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) Antiviral Drug Discovery (AViDD) Center, the Denver Foundation, the Novo Nordisk Foundation, the Stanford Bio-X Program and a Bio-X Interdisciplinary Graduate Student Fellowship, E&M Foundation Postdoctoral Fellowship, Postdoctoral Fellowship in Translational Medicine from the PhRMA Foundation and an anonymous donation to establish the Stanford BSL3 facility. The research used resources at SSRL, a DOE Office of Science user facility, and of the SSRL Structural Molecular Biology Program supported by the DOE Office of Biological and Environmental Research and by NIH National Institute of General Medical Sciences. Publications Westberg, M., et al. “An orally bioavailable SARS-CoV-2 main protease inhibitor exhibits improved affinity and reduced sensitivity to mutations”, Sci. Transl. Med. 16, eadi0979 (2024). The research was supported by multiple funding sources, including the National Institute of Health and Stanford University. While the development is promising, no specific implementation or distribution details have been provided, and the research is ongoing. This innovation highlights the potential for repurposing existing drugs to address emerging challenges in the fight against the pandemic.

Circulation Cases Deaths Hospitalizations Vaccines Variants Wastewater Data About More resources More COVID-19 Cases, %%COUNTRY%% WHO will utilize various sources to continue monitoring the COVID-19 epidemiological situation via the WHO COVID-19 dashboard. If data for certain countries is unavailable in this section, it may indicate that they have either ceased reporting COVID-19 surveillance data to WHO or have integrated the COVID-19 surveillance into existing respiratory disease surveillance. In the latter case, SARS-CoV-2 detections from sentinel and systematic virological surveillance sites in those countries may be found in the Circulation section which also includes information on SARS-CoV-2 variant circulation. This global summary of COVID-19 cases includes data on confirmed cases reported to WHO from the comprehensive COVID-19 case monitoring. Coronavirus (COVID-19) cases, %%COUNTRY%% data Source: World Health Organization Loading... Loading... Loading... What is the definition of 'confirmed' and 'reported' in COVID-19 data? All data represents the date of reporting as opposed to date of symptom onset. All data is subject to continuous verification and may change based on retrospective updates to accurately reflect trends, changes in country case definitions and/or reporting practices. Significant data errors detected or reported to WHO may be corrected at more frequent intervals with some countries performing retrospective bulk corrections may lead to the appearance of significant spikes or negative values which are verified and validated by WHO. In the context of WHO's statistical reporting of COVID-19 data, it is important to note that only confirmed cases are included in case and death counts. In guidance updated on 22 July 2023; there are two alternative definitions for 'Confirmed case of SARS-CoV-2 infection' in international surveillance reporting, although some departures may exist due to local adaptations: a) A person with a positive Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT), regardless of clinical criteria OR epidemiological criteria. b) A person meeting clinical criteria AND/OR epidemiological criteria (suspect case A) with a positive professional-use or self-test SARS-CoV-2 Antigen-RDT. Additionally, WHO only disseminates data as reported by its Member States. From the 31 December 2019 to the 21 March 2020, WHO collected the numbers of confirmed COVID-19 cases and deaths through official communications under the International Health Regulations (IHR, 2005), complemented by monitoring the official ministries of health websites and social media accounts. Since 22 March 2020, global data has been compiled through WHO region-specific dashboards, and/or aggregate count data reported directly to WHO headquarters by Member States. Statistical counts include both domestic and repatriated cases. Case detection, definitions, testing strategies, reporting practice, and lag times (e.g. time to case notification, and time to reporting of deaths) differ between countries, territories and areas. These factors, amongst others, influence the counts presented with variable under or overestimation of true case and death counts, and variable delays to reflecting these statistics at a global level. Please note that statistics do not necessarily reflect the actual number of cases and deaths or the actual number of countries where cases and deaths are occurring, as a number of countries have stopped reporting or changed their frequency of reporting. Trends in COVID-19 cases, %%COUNTRY%% Recent COVID-19 cases reported to WHO (weekly) %%COUNTRY%%, July 2023 - present Source: World Health Organization Data may be incomplete for the latest week. Total COVID-19 cases reported to WHO (weekly) %%COUNTRY%%, January 2020 - present Source: World Health Organization Why is COVID-19 data being presented as weekly statistics? A number of countries have stopped reporting or changed their frequency of reporting COVID-19 case and death counts to WHO. An outcome of these differences in reporting is that WHO may receive daily data from some countries, while other countries may only report data to WHO once every 14 days. In addition, countries differ in how they choose to report statistics; some countries provide their data attributed to specific dates while others who report less frequently may group data from 7 days into a single statistic attributed to a week in their reporting. As of 25 August 2023, WHO declared that it is no longer necessary for Member States to report daily counts of cases and deaths to WHO and requested strengthening of weekly reporting. Reported data is still available attributed to specific dates (daily data) here as a download. This dashboard presents the same statistics as weekly figures in charts in order to mitigate against the visual misinterpretation of data. Should daily data have been presented here, many countries would show zero counts for multiple consecutive days due in part to the differences in how they choose to report. While weekly intervals do not completely mitigate against this, the approach reduces the risk that some dashboard users might infer zero cases or deaths when lack of data is often due to reporting differences. What do negative counts of cases or deaths mean? All data is subject to continuous verification and may change based on retrospective updates to accurately reflect trends, changes in country case definitions and/or reporting practices. Significant data errors detected or reported to WHO may be corrected by Member States at more frequent intervals with some countries performing retrospective bulk corrections in their reporting. Bulk corrections may lead to the appearance of significant spikes or negative values which are verified and validated by WHO. Aggregate groups (weekly data to week end date) Source: World Health Organization COVID-19 cases, country level trends Percent change based on previous 28 days Source: World Health Organization Metadata Glossary and definitions Confirmed COVID-19 case Although COVID-19 defines the symptomatic disease caused by SARS-CoV-2, the cases are presented in this dashboard meet one of two alternate definitions of confirmed case of SARS-CoV-2 infection in international surveillance reporting: a) A person with a positive Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT), regardless of clinical criteria* OR epidemiological criteria*. b) A person meeting clinical criteria* AND/OR epidemiological criteria* (suspect case A) with a positive professional-use or self-test SARS-CoV-2 Antigen-RDT. *Please visit the WHO COVID-19 Case definition for details on clinical and epidemiological criteria. Updated 22 July 2023 Last 7 days ‘Last 7 days’ refers to the most recent complete epidemiological week (commonly referred to as an 'epi week'). Last 28 days ‘Last 28 days’ refers to the four preceding most recently complete epidemiological weeks. WHO Regions The World Health Organization (WHO) is divided into six regions with regional offices, each responsible for addressing health challenges and promoting public health within its designated geographical area. These regions serve as administrative units that allow the WHO to tailor its efforts to the specific needs, priorities, and health conditions of member countries within each region. World Bank Income Groups The World Bank classifies economies into income groups based on their Gross National Income (GNI) per capita. These annually updated classifications help the World Bank and other organizations analyze and understand global economic trends, allocate resources, and design development policies. Data sources COVID-19 case data From the 31 December 2019 to the 21 March 2020, WHO collected the numbers of confirmed COVID-19 cases and deaths through official communications under the International Health Regulations (IHR, 2005), complemented by monitoring the official ministries of health websites and social media accounts. Since 22 March 2020, global data is compiled through WHO region-specific dashboards, and/or aggregate count data reported to WHO headquarters. WHO COVID-19 Dashboard is updated every Tuesday for the period of two full weeks prior. Counts primarily reflect laboratory-confirmed cases and deaths, based upon WHO case definitions; although some departures may exist due to local adaptations. Counts include both domestic and repatriated cases. Case detection, definitions, testing strategies, reporting practice, and lag times (e.g. time to case notification, and time to reporting of deaths) differ between countries, territories and areas. These factors, amongst others, influence the counts presented with variable under or overestimation of true case and death counts, and variable delays to reflecting these data at a global level. All data represent date of reporting as opposed to date of symptom onset. All data are subject to continuous verification and may change based on retrospective updates to accurately reflect trends, changes in country case definitions and/or reporting practices. Significant data errors detected or reported to WHO may be corrected at more frequent intervals. New case and death counts from the Region of the Americas Starting from the week commencing on 11 September 2023, the source of the data from the Region of the Americas was switched to the aggregated national surveillances, received through the COVID-19, Influenza, RSV and Other Respiratory Viruses program in the Americas. Data have been included retrospectively since 31 July 2023. Rates <0.001 per 100,000 population may be rounded to 0. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Monday, November 23, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Biology SARS-CoV-2 JN.1 Variant Persisted Longer in Pakistan Than in Western Nations by November 22, 2026 in Biology Reading Time: 7 mins read 0 SARS-CoV-2 JN.1 Variant Persisted Longer in Pakistan Than in Western Nations Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A retrospective genomic surveillance investigation analyzing severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 isolates collected across Pakistan between January 2023 and September 2024 has uncovered distinct regional evolutionary trajectories, highlighted by the prolonged persistence of the JN.1 Omicron lineage compared with patterns observed in Western nations. Conducted by an interdisciplinary team of researchers from Aga Khan University in Karachi and published in the Brazilian Journal of Microbiology, the study evaluated the post-pandemic diversification of viral lineages following the formal conclusion of the global public health emergency. While high-income Western countries experienced rapid lineage turnovers where JN.1 was swiftly displaced by newer sub-lineages such as KP.3.1.1 by mid-2024, circulating viral populations in Pakistan demonstrated an extended duration of JN.1 dominance that lasted through the third quarter of 2024. This sustained prevalence occurred alongside substantial genomic entropy, offering valuable empirical insights into how regional transmission patterns, diagnostic infrastructure, and baseline population exposures modulate SARS-CoV-2 molecular evolution across diverse geographic environments. The central research objective focused on addressing substantial knowledge gaps concerning post-2023 SARS-CoV-2 molecular epidemiology within South Asia, where systematic genomic surveillance has historically been constrained relative to high-throughput surveillance programs in North America and Western Europe. To investigate how circulating lineages in Pakistan compared against international benchmarks, the investigators accessed public sequence repositories alongside clinical diagnostic specimens to analyze phylogenetic diversity, nucleotide substitution rates, and positional entropy across the viral genome. By establishing a rigorous comparative framework that contrasted Pakistani viral sequences against standardized cohorts from the United States, the United Kingdom, France, and neighboring India, the researchers sought to determine whether post-pandemic viral populations followed a synchronized global trajectory or diverged in response to local epidemiological conditions. The resulting analyses demonstrate that while basic evolutionary mechanisms and substitution kinetics remain broadly comparable across continents, the actual composition and temporal persistence of dominant clades can vary markedly across jurisdictions. Discover more Tour Colleges Study Biology Study Chemistry To construct their primary observational dataset, the investigators retrieved genomic records deposited in the Global Initiative on Sharing All Influenza Data EpiCoV database between January 2023 and September 2024, filtering for complete genomes that exhibited more than 95 percent sequence coverage, fewer than 1 percent ambiguous nucleotide calls, and verified collection dates and regional metadata. From an initial national download of 976 SARS-CoV-2 genomes from Pakistan, the researchers excluded travel-associated cases and duplicate entries, ultimately grouping 41 low-frequency lineages according to their designated Nextstrain clades while preserving overarching phylogenetic relationships to yield a focused dataset of 935 representative genomes for temporal analysis. Temporal coverage within this national repository varied across the surveillance timeframe, with sequencing frequency reaching its highest peak in March 2023 with 343 analyzed genomes, followed by a secondary peak of 109 genomes in March 2024, reflecting operational realities where routine molecular testing ebbed and flowed alongside fluctuating clinical demand. Discover more Engineering Job Board Research Paper Access Learn Engineering Track Biotech Complementing the national GISAID sequence repository, the research team conducted an in-depth retrospective laboratory evaluation of 282 nasopharyngeal swab specimens confirmed positive for SARS-CoV-2 via reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction assays at the Aga Khan University Hospital Clinical Laboratories. Because the hospital operates a diagnostic network comprising more than 300 sample collection centers distributed throughout Pakistan, the laboratory cohort provided access to standardized clinical testing data and patient demographics that are frequently absent from international public sequence databases. Diagnostic screening was performed using the automated Roche Cobas 6800 system targeting the Orf1ab genetic region, and positive samples demonstrating cycle threshold values of 35 or lower were systematically charted to observe local testing trends. Of these confirmed diagnostic specimens, a subset of 223 samples satisfied the stringent quality criteria established for whole genome sequencing, which required a cycle threshold value of 26 or below to ensure sufficient template density for high-throughput multiplex library construction. The methodological workflow for clinical sequencing involved reverse transcribing viral ribonucleic acid into complementary DNA using specialized commercial synthesis kits, followed by dual-pool multiplex PCR amplification using validated ARTIC network version 3 primers designed specifically for SARS-CoV-2 genome recovery. Amplicons were converted into sequencing libraries using Illumina Nextera DNA Flex protocols and subsequently resolved on an Illumina MiSeq sequencing platform. Bioinformatic processing was carried out via the cloud-based CZID computational platform, which filtered out human host reads using minimap2 alignments against the human reference genome before aligning residual reads against the ancestral Wuhan-Hu-1 reference sequence NC_045512.2. Adaptor sequences were removed using Trim Galore, base calls were strictly retained only when sequence depth exceeded 10-fold coverage, and consensus variants were identified using samtools and BCFtools v1.20 to ensure analytical fidelity prior to downstream phylogenetic reconstruction. Phylogenetic lineage designations for the assembled genomes were systematically assigned using the Pangolin tool with the pangoLEARN algorithmic model, while Nextstrain clade classifications and amino acid substitutions were verified through Nextclade version 3.5.0. Multiple sequence alignments of complete viral genomes were generated using MAFFT version 7.505, after which maximum-likelihood phylogenetic trees were constructed utilizing IQ-TREE version 2.2.0 parameterized under the general time-reversible model with gamma-distributed rate heterogeneity across sites. Evolutionary rates and branch lengths were computed using the Augur bioinformatics pipeline and TreeTime within a time-resolved framework, where molecular clock outliers were filtered using a four-times interquartile range threshold. To assess site-specific amino acid variability, positional Shannon entropy across all ten open reading frames was calculated mathematically based on the relative frequencies of observed residues, with visual representations generated in Auspice, FigTree, and custom R scripts. For international comparisons, the authors assembled global datasets from the United States, the United Kingdom, France, and India over the identical twenty-one-month surveillance window. Because raw submission counts in GISAID were heavily skewed—ranging from 286,135 sequences from the United States to 14,734 sequences from India—the authors executed a monthly down-sampling algorithm to standardize statistical comparisons. Specifically, custom Python routines selected up to 300 representative genomes per country-month, retaining all available sequences whenever monthly submissions fell below that threshold. This normalization strategy generated standardized comparison datasets consisting of 6,300 genomes each for the United States, the United Kingdom, and France, alongside 3,435 genomes for India. Combining these standardized international cohorts with 780 representative Pakistani genomes enabled the construction of a comprehensive, time-resolved maximum-likelihood tree spanning Nextstrain clades 21L through 24E, providing an empirical basis for comparing lineage turnover and evolutionary rates across disparate health systems. Analysis of national lineage dynamics in Pakistan revealed a clear temporal progression among 86 distinct identified variants, though only 13 achieved relative monthly frequencies exceeding 20 percent. During the first half of 2023, viral populations were heavily dominated by recombinant XBB lineages, particularly XBB.1.19.1 and XBB.1.9.1, which collectively accounted for 39 percent of characterized genomes in March 2023. By August 2023, these ancestral recombinants were replaced by emerging sub-lineages GW.5, GW.5.1, and persistent XBB.1.19.1 strains, before transitioning toward FL.1 and FY.5 by October 2023. The pivotal evolutionary transition occurred in late 2023 with the introduction of the BA.2.86-descended variant JN.1. Unlike Western comparison countries, where JN.1 was rapidly superseded by newer progeny such as KP.3.1.1 during the spring and summer of 2024, Pakistan experienced prolonged JN.1 dominance throughout the surveillance window, with JN.1 and its sub-lineage JN.1.18 representing 77 percent of sequenced isolates in March 2024 and remaining predominant through September 2024 despite sporadic detections of KP.2, LB.1, and LA.1. Demographic and epidemiological evaluations performed on 213 sequenced samples at the Aga Khan University Hospital revealed that the vast majority of analyzed specimens originated from Sindh province, with Karachi and Hyderabad accounting for 94.8 percent of cases, alongside sporadic submissions from Punjab, Islamabad Capital Territory, Gilgit-Baltistan, Baluchistan, and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Patient age distributions indicated that adults aged 19 to 50 years comprised 54 percent of positive cases, older adults aged over 50 years represented 44 percent, and pediatric individuals aged 1 to 18 years accounted for 3 percent. Statistical evaluations revealed no significant linear trend in case numbers across the study period via chi-square testing, reflecting intermittent wave-like epidemic surges rather than continuous increases. Furthermore, categorical analysis of 21 lineages across patient characteristics demonstrated no statistically significant associations between specific SARS-CoV-2 lineages and patient gender via Fisher’s exact test, patient age categories via chi-square analysis, or inpatient versus outpatient clinical status. When assessing molecular clock kinetics, the estimated nucleotide substitution rate for SARS-CoV-2 in Pakistan was calculated at 4.67 times 10 to the negative fourth power substitutions per site per year, accompanied by a 95 percent confidence interval extending from 3.29 times 10 to the negative fourth power to 6.04 times 10 to the negative fourth power. This measured substitution rate was statistically indistinguishable from the rates calculated for Western nations, where point estimates ranged between 4.4 times 10 to the negative fourth power and 5.22 times 10 to the negative fourth power per site per year. Formal meta-analytic evaluation using Cochran’s Q test confirmed an absence of significant overall heterogeneity among substitution rates observed in Pakistan, the United States, the United Kingdom, and France. In contrast, genomes analyzed from India exhibited a significantly lower estimated substitution rate of 6.92 times 10 to the negative fifth power per site per year, though this figure was accompanied by an unusually wide confidence interval ranging from zero to 1.4 times 10 to the negative fourth power, suggesting underlying data constraints or differences in lineage sampling rather than true biological divergence. Genomic diversity analyses revealed that SARS-CoV-2 isolates in Pakistan exhibited a mean positional Shannon entropy of 0.0324 across the complete coding sequence, a figure noticeably higher than the baseline positional entropy values recorded for the United States at 0.0100, the United Kingdom at 0.0107, France at 0.0105, and India at 0.0129. Across all examined geographical regions, mutational density was consistently concentrated within the spike glycoprotein gene region, followed by open reading frame 1ab and the membrane protein gene, aligning with known selective pressures directed against viral surface antigens. While the elevated genomic entropy observed in Pakistan mirrors findings from prolonged national surveillance in other settings where post-outbreak diversification accumulates, the study authors explicitly noted that this elevated metric could partially reflect sampling dynamics inherent to smaller, geographically concentrated datasets rather than purely elevated viral mutation rates in vivo. Interpretation of these epidemiological findings must be framed within several methodological and structural limitations acknowledged by the investigators. First, the total volume of genomic sequencing performed in Pakistan was modest compared to high-resource nations, driven by constrained diagnostic resources where national testing capacity peaked at approximately 46,500 tests daily during 2021 compared to 1 million daily tests in the United States. Second, because clinical severity metrics and vaccination histories were unavailable for the vast majority of sequenced isolates, the authors could not directly correlate specific lineage replacements with clinical outcomes or immune breakthrough frequencies. Third, geographic representation was heavily skewed toward Sindh province due to the centralized location of the sequencing infrastructure in Karachi, leaving rural provinces underrepresented. Despite these constraints, the study provides foundational documentation of post-pandemic viral evolution in Pakistan, illustrating how regional vaccine platforms—dominated by inactivated formulations such as Sinopharm and SinoVac—alongside distinct population demographics can foster localized evolutionary niches that sustain major viral lineages long after their global displacement. supplementary_news.content_title: Current booster vaccine protects against new PJ.2.1 SARS-CoV-2 variant
supplementary_news.content: Germany's COVID-19 traffic light is on red ( https://corona-ampel.de/ ), and the number of infections is high. But how well is the population protected against the virus variants currently circulating? The new SARS-CoV-2 variant PJ.2.1 has been spreading since May and has long since reached Europe. It traces back to an older viral lineage that has since largely disappeared from the infection landscape. However, the virus likely persisted in a person with a long-term infection and underwent significant changes through numerous mutations. Researchers from the Infection Biology Unit at the German Primate Center - Leibniz Institute for Primate Research, in collaboration with colleagues from Hannover Medical School, investigated how efficiently PJ.2.1 can penetrate human cells and how well antibodies from vaccinated individuals neutralize the new variant. The results show that PJ.2.1 binds more strongly than the other virus variants studied to the ACE2 receptor, which serves as the entry point for SARS-CoV-2 into human cells, and enters certain cells that produce only small amounts of ACE2 more effectively. Despite these changes, the new variant was effectively neutralized by antibodies produced following vaccination with the current booster vaccine, which has been adapted to the XFG variant. The results suggest that vaccination provides protection against PJ.2.1. However, this could change if the variant acquires additional mutations that enable it to evade the immune response (Journal of Infection, The Lancet Infectious Diseases). A hallmark of SARS-CoV-2 is the continuous emergence of new viral variants with changes in the spike protein, which allow the virus to partially evade the antibody response. Often, such variants differ from their predecessors by only a few mutations in the spike protein. These can alter binding sites for antibodies and/or influence binding to the ACE2 receptor, which the virus uses to enter human cells. In addition, however, variants may also emerge that are characterized by an unusually large number of mutations - particularly in the spike protein - and thus evade the existing antibody response particularly efficiently. Such so-called saltation variants can develop during long-term infections. In this process, the virus has the opportunity over an extended period to replicate within the body of an infected person and gradually undergo significant changes. Since May 2026, a new saltation variant of SARS-CoV-2 has been spreading: PJ.2.1. The variant was first detected in Canada and subsequently spread to the United States. Until now, it was unclear how efficiently PJ.2.1 can penetrate cells and how susceptible the variant is to neutralizing antibodies . In particular, it was not known how effectively antibodies produced following vaccination can inhibit PJ.2.1. A research team led by infection biologists Markus Hoffmann and Stefan Pöhlmann from the German Primate Center - Leibniz Institute for Primate Research, in collaboration with Georg Behrens's research group at Hannover Medical School, investigated these questions. Their findings show that PJ.2.1 is spreading rapidly in Canada, the U.S., and Spain; its prevalence is also rising in the Netherlands and France. A spread in Germany is therefore to be expected. With infection rates remaining high overall, the variant has been detected in all age groups. There is currently no evidence of more severe disease progression or new symptoms compared to other SARS-CoV-2 variants. The researchers found that the spike protein of PJ.2.1 binds more strongly to ACE2. Consistent with this, PJ.2.1 was better able than other variants to penetrate cells that produce only small amounts of the ACE2 receptor. PJ.2.1 was effectively inhibited by antibodies from individuals who had been vaccinated with the XFG-adapted mRNA vaccine Comirnaty, which is currently in use in Germany. In contrast, the SARS-CoV-2 variant BA.3.2, which is primarily detected in children, was only inadequately inhibited by these antibodies. Our results suggest that PJ.2.1 is likely spreading worldwide due to improved ACE2 binding. We assume that the XFG-adapted vaccine provides effective protection against PJ.2.1 as well as against the XFG viruses that are also circulating - at least as long as these viruses do not acquire mutations that allow them to evade the antibody response more effectively." Markus Hoffmann, German Primate Center - Leibniz Institute for Primate Research Stefan Pöhlmann adds: "Notably, neither the vaccine used last season nor the currently available vaccine elicits an antibody response that efficiently blocks BA.3.2 from entering cells. Since BA.3.2 is detected primarily in children, it should be investigated whether an additional component tailored to this variant could be included in future COVID-19 vaccines." Source: Journal reference: Happle, C., et al . (2026). Humoral immunity after mRNA SARS-CoV-2 XFG vaccination. The Lancet Infectious Diseases . DOI: 10.1016/s1473-3099(26)00569-4. https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laninf/article/PIIS1473-3099(26)00569-4/fulltext
