supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Monday, November 23, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Biology SARS-CoV-2 JN.1 Variant Persisted Longer in Pakistan Than in Western Nations by November 22, 2026 in Biology Reading Time: 7 mins read 0 SARS-CoV-2 JN.1 Variant Persisted Longer in Pakistan Than in Western Nations Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A retrospective genomic surveillance investigation analyzing severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 isolates collected across Pakistan between January 2023 and September 2024 has uncovered distinct regional evolutionary trajectories, highlighted by the prolonged persistence of the JN.1 Omicron lineage compared with patterns observed in Western nations. Conducted by an interdisciplinary team of researchers from Aga Khan University in Karachi and published in the Brazilian Journal of Microbiology, the study evaluated the post-pandemic diversification of viral lineages following the formal conclusion of the global public health emergency. While high-income Western countries experienced rapid lineage turnovers where JN.1 was swiftly displaced by newer sub-lineages such as KP.3.1.1 by mid-2024, circulating viral populations in Pakistan demonstrated an extended duration of JN.1 dominance that lasted through the third quarter of 2024. This sustained prevalence occurred alongside substantial genomic entropy, offering valuable empirical insights into how regional transmission patterns, diagnostic infrastructure, and baseline population exposures modulate SARS-CoV-2 molecular evolution across diverse geographic environments. The central research objective focused on addressing substantial knowledge gaps concerning post-2023 SARS-CoV-2 molecular epidemiology within South Asia, where systematic genomic surveillance has historically been constrained relative to high-throughput surveillance programs in North America and Western Europe. To investigate how circulating lineages in Pakistan compared against international benchmarks, the investigators accessed public sequence repositories alongside clinical diagnostic specimens to analyze phylogenetic diversity, nucleotide substitution rates, and positional entropy across the viral genome. By establishing a rigorous comparative framework that contrasted Pakistani viral sequences against standardized cohorts from the United States, the United Kingdom, France, and neighboring India, the researchers sought to determine whether post-pandemic viral populations followed a synchronized global trajectory or diverged in response to local epidemiological conditions. The resulting analyses demonstrate that while basic evolutionary mechanisms and substitution kinetics remain broadly comparable across continents, the actual composition and temporal persistence of dominant clades can vary markedly across jurisdictions. To construct their primary observational dataset, the investigators retrieved genomic records deposited in the Global Initiative on Sharing All Influenza Data EpiCoV database between January 2023 and September 2024, filtering for complete genomes that exhibited more than 95 percent sequence coverage, fewer than 1 percent ambiguous nucleotide calls, and verified collection dates and regional metadata. From an initial national download of 976 SARS-CoV-2 genomes from Pakistan, the researchers excluded travel-associated cases and duplicate entries, ultimately grouping 41 low-frequency lineages according to their designated Nextstrain clades while preserving overarching phylogenetic relationships to yield a focused dataset of 935 representative genomes for temporal analysis. Temporal coverage within this national repository varied across the surveillance timeframe, with sequencing frequency reaching its highest peak in March 2023 with 343 analyzed genomes, followed by a secondary peak of 109 genomes in March 2024, reflecting operational realities where routine molecular testing ebbed and flowed alongside fluctuating clinical demand. Complementing the national GISAID sequence repository, the research team conducted an in-depth retrospective laboratory evaluation of 282 nasopharyngeal swab specimens confirmed positive for SARS-CoV-2 via reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction assays at the Aga Khan University Hospital Clinical Laboratories. Because the hospital operates a diagnostic network comprising more than 300 sample collection centers distributed throughout Pakistan, the laboratory cohort provided access to standardized clinical testing data and patient demographics that are frequently absent from international public sequence databases. Diagnostic screening was performed using the automated Roche Cobas 6800 system targeting the Orf1ab genetic region, and positive samples demonstrating cycle threshold values of 35 or lower were systematically charted to observe local testing trends. Of these confirmed diagnostic specimens, a subset of 223 samples satisfied the stringent quality criteria established for whole genome sequencing, which required a cycle threshold value of 26 or below to ensure sufficient template density for high-throughput multiplex library construction. The methodological workflow for clinical sequencing involved reverse transcribing viral ribonucleic acid into complementary DNA using specialized commercial synthesis kits, followed by dual-pool multiplex PCR amplification using validated ARTIC network version 3 primers designed specifically for SARS-CoV-2 genome recovery. Amplicons were converted into sequencing libraries using Illumina Nextera DNA Flex protocols and subsequently resolved on an Illumina MiSeq sequencing platform. Bioinformatic processing was carried out via the cloud-based CZID computational platform, which filtered out human host reads using minimap2 alignments against the human reference genome before aligning residual reads against the ancestral Wuhan-Hu-1 reference sequence NC_045512.2. Adaptor sequences were removed using Trim Galore, base calls were strictly retained only when sequence depth exceeded 10-fold coverage, and consensus variants were identified using samtools and BCFtools v1.20 to ensure analytical fidelity prior to downstream phylogenetic reconstruction. Phylogenetic lineage designations for the assembled genomes were systematically assigned using the Pangolin tool with the pangoLEARN algorithmic model, while Nextstrain clade classifications and amino acid substitutions were verified through Nextclade version 3.5.0. Multiple sequence alignments of complete viral genomes were generated using MAFFT version 7.505, after which maximum-likelihood phylogenetic trees were constructed utilizing IQ-TREE version 2.2.0 parameterized under the general time-reversible model with gamma-distributed rate heterogeneity across sites. Evolutionary rates and branch lengths were computed using the Augur bioinformatics pipeline and TreeTime within a time-resolved framework, where molecular clock outliers were filtered using a four-times interquartile range threshold. To assess site-specific amino acid variability, positional Shannon entropy across all ten open reading frames was calculated mathematically based on the relative frequencies of observed residues, with visual representations generated in Auspice, FigTree, and custom R scripts. For international comparisons, the authors assembled global datasets from the United States, the United Kingdom, France, and India over the identical twenty-one-month surveillance window. Because raw submission counts in GISAID were heavily skewed—ranging from 286,135 sequences from the United States to 14,734 sequences from India—the authors executed a monthly down-sampling algorithm to standardize statistical comparisons. Specifically, custom Python routines selected up to 300 representative genomes per country-month, retaining all available sequences whenever monthly submissions fell below that threshold. This normalization strategy generated standardized comparison datasets consisting of 6,300 genomes each for the United States, the United Kingdom, and France, alongside 3,435 genomes for India. Combining these standardized international cohorts with 780 representative Pakistani genomes enabled the construction of a comprehensive, time-resolved maximum-likelihood tree spanning Nextstrain clades 21L through 24E, providing an empirical basis for comparing lineage turnover and evolutionary rates across disparate health systems. Analysis of national lineage dynamics in Pakistan revealed a clear temporal progression among 86 distinct identified variants, though only 13 achieved relative monthly frequencies exceeding 20 percent. During the first half of 2023, viral populations were heavily dominated by recombinant XBB lineages, particularly XBB.1.19.1 and XBB.1.9.1, which collectively accounted for 39 percent of characterized genomes in March 2023. By August 2023, these ancestral recombinants were replaced by emerging sub-lineages GW.5, GW.5.1, and persistent XBB.1.19.1 strains, before transitioning toward FL.1 and FY.5 by October 2023. The pivotal evolutionary transition occurred in late 2023 with the introduction of the BA.2.86-descended variant JN.1. Unlike Western comparison countries, where JN.1 was rapidly superseded by newer progeny such as KP.3.1.1 during the spring and summer of 2024, Pakistan experienced prolonged JN.1 dominance throughout the surveillance window, with JN.1 and its sub-lineage JN.1.18 representing 77 percent of sequenced isolates in March 2024 and remaining predominant through September 2024 despite sporadic detections of KP.2, LB.1, and LA.1. Demographic and epidemiological evaluations performed on 213 sequenced samples at the Aga Khan University Hospital revealed that the vast majority of analyzed specimens originated from Sindh province, with Karachi and Hyderabad accounting for 94.8 percent of cases, alongside sporadic submissions from Punjab, Islamabad Capital Territory, Gilgit-Baltistan, Baluchistan, and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Patient age distributions indicated that adults aged 19 to 50 years comprised 54 percent of positive cases, older adults aged over 50 years represented 44 percent, and pediatric individuals aged 1 to 18 years accounted for 3 percent. Statistical evaluations revealed no significant linear trend in case numbers across the study period via chi-square testing, reflecting intermittent wave-like epidemic surges rather than continuous increases. Furthermore, categorical analysis of 21 lineages across patient characteristics demonstrated no statistically significant associations between specific SARS-CoV-2 lineages and patient gender via Fisher’s exact test, patient age categories via chi-square analysis, or inpatient versus outpatient clinical status. When assessing molecular clock kinetics, the estimated nucleotide substitution rate for SARS-CoV-2 in Pakistan was calculated at 4.67 times 10 to the negative fourth power substitutions per site per year, accompanied by a 95 percent confidence interval extending from 3.29 times 10 to the negative fourth power to 6.04 times 10 to the negative fourth power. This measured substitution rate was statistically indistinguishable from the rates calculated for Western nations, where point estimates ranged between 4.4 times 10 to the negative fourth power and 5.22 times 10 to the negative fourth power per site per year. Formal meta-analytic evaluation using Cochran’s Q test confirmed an absence of significant overall heterogeneity among substitution rates observed in Pakistan, the United States, the United Kingdom, and France. In contrast, genomes analyzed from India exhibited a significantly lower estimated substitution rate of 6.92 times 10 to the negative fifth power per site per year, though this figure was accompanied by an unusually wide confidence interval ranging from zero to 1.4 times 10 to the negative fourth power, suggesting underlying data constraints or differences in lineage sampling rather than true biological divergence. Genomic diversity analyses revealed that SARS-CoV-2 isolates in Pakistan exhibited a mean positional Shannon entropy of 0.0324 across the complete coding sequence, a figure noticeably higher than the baseline positional entropy values recorded for the United States at 0.0100, the United Kingdom at 0.0107, France at 0.0105, and India at 0.0129. Across all examined geographical regions, mutational density was consistently concentrated within the spike glycoprotein gene region, followed by open reading frame 1ab and the membrane protein gene, aligning with known selective pressures directed against viral surface antigens. While the elevated genomic entropy observed in Pakistan mirrors findings from prolonged national surveillance in other settings where post-outbreak diversification accumulates, the study authors explicitly noted that this elevated metric could partially reflect sampling dynamics inherent to smaller, geographically concentrated datasets rather than purely elevated viral mutation rates in vivo. Interpretation of these epidemiological findings must be framed within several methodological and structural limitations acknowledged by the investigators. First, the total volume of genomic sequencing performed in Pakistan was modest compared to high-resource nations, driven by constrained diagnostic resources where national testing capacity peaked at approximately 46,500 tests daily during 2021 compared to 1 million daily tests in the United States. Second, because clinical severity metrics and vaccination histories were unavailable for the vast majority of sequenced isolates, the authors could not directly correlate specific lineage replacements with clinical outcomes or immune breakthrough frequencies. Third, geographic representation was heavily skewed toward Sindh province due to the centralized location of the sequencing infrastructure in Karachi, leaving rural provinces underrepresented. Despite these constraints, the study provides foundational documentation of post-pandemic viral evolution in Pakistan, illustrating how regional vaccine platforms—dominated by inactivated formulations such as Sinopharm and SinoVac—alongside distinct population demographics can foster localized evolutionary niches that sustain major viral lineages long after their global displacement. The case report, published in Laboratory Animal Research, documents a solitary round cell neoplasm within the brain of a 19-week-old male k18-hACE2 mouse that had been inoculated intranasally with the virus as part of an experimental investigation. Microscopic and molecular examinations revealed viral antigens localized directly inside tumor-associated histiocytes and adjacent cortical neurons, providing an initial documented observation of SARS-CoV-2 tropism within a primary central nervous system tumor in this animal model. Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 is recognized primarily as a respiratory pathogen causing coronavirus disease 2019, but neurological manifestations frequently accompany acute infection. Reported complications in humans include headache, anosmia, encephalitis, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, Guillain-Barré syndrome, seizures, delirium, dementia-like syndromes, and psychiatric disorders, reflecting the neuroinvasive capability of the pathogen. Neurological signs and tissue lesions have been reported in 36.4 percent of human patients who succumbed to COVID-19. Cellular neuroinvasion is linked to the presence of human angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 receptors, which are widely expressed throughout the central nervous system across neurons, microglia, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes, in addition to epithelial linings of the respiratory and digestive tracts. To evaluate viral dynamics and neuropathology, researchers commonly utilize the k18-hACE2 transgenic mouse strain, in which human ACE2 expression is driven under the control of the cytokeratin 18 promoter. This transgenic lineage develops substantial viral neuroinvasion, severe encephalitis, and elevated mortality following viral exposure. While previous investigations have explored whether viral infections modulate cancer initiation or accelerate malignant progression, primary histiocytic and lymphoproliferative disorders of the central nervous system remain exceptionally rare in laboratory mice. Primary central nervous system lymphomas account for aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphomas, with diffuse large B-cell lymphomas representing 90 percent of human cases, often associated with immune dysfunction or oncogenic viruses such as Epstein-Barr virus and human immunodeficiency virus. Discover more Infection infection Check Symptoms infections Study Biology The affected male mouse was housed within biosafety level 3 facilities at the VISAVET health surveillance center and challenged intranasally with a viral suspension of 25 microliters containing 10,000 tissue culture infectious doses (50 percent end point). The animal was monitored daily for clinical progression, including changes in body weight, coat condition, activity levels, eye closure, and respiratory or neurological distress. By the seventh day post-infection, marked clinical deterioration was evident, characterized by pronounced inactivity, closed eyes, and a 10 percent loss in body weight, prompting humane euthanasia. Post-mortem examination and comprehensive necropsy were conducted immediately to recover organs for quantitative virological evaluation and full-body histopathology. Viral quantification was conducted on recovered tissues using a reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction assay with confirmed sensitivity down to 10 viral copies. The initial viral inoculum registered a concentration of 1.94 million copies per microliter. Within harvested animal tissues at seven days post-infection, viral burden reached 165,000 copies per microliter in brain tissue, compared to 120 copies per microliter in the lungs and 260 copies per microliter in the trachea and nasal turbinates. These measurements demonstrated significant viral replication and high tropism within the central nervous system compartment relative to the primary respiratory entry sites. Gross anatomical inspection revealed focal pulmonary congestion accompanied by dark reddish areas of consolidation in the cranial lung lobes, while other major visceral organs appeared grossly unremarkable. Histopathological examination of the respiratory tract identified bronchointerstitial pneumonia accompanied by epithelial hyperplasia of bronchioles and type II pneumocytes, with evidence of mild perivascular edema and focal vascular thrombosis. Histological analysis of non-neural peripheral organs confirmed the absence of metastatic lesions, indicating that the intracranial mass was a primary, solitary neoplasm originating within the central nervous system. Microscopic evaluation of brain sections stained with hematoxylin and eosin demonstrated an oval, well-demarcated leptomeningeal tumor positioned over the secondary somatosensory cortex within the diencephalic subdivision. The mass measured 1,340 micrometers in length by 590 micrometers in width and was completely enveloped by a thin fibroblastic capsule. The neoplastic mass exhibited moderate neovascularization and a mild to moderate presence of mitotic figures. Cellular composition comprised dense accumulations of mononuclear round cells resembling lymphoblasts with indented nuclei, intermixed with larger atypical lymphocytes and abundant, paler histiocytic cells featuring prominent nucleoli. Discover more infectious Find Cancer Care Try Brain Games Study Anatomy Find Neurologists The surrounding brain parenchyma presented acute histopathological changes characteristic of severe neuroinvasive viral infection. Sections exhibited diffuse meningoencephalitis, perivascular lymphocytic cuffing, widespread vasculitis, increased glial cell proliferation, and vacuolation along white matter myelin tracts. Cortical neurons displayed degenerative alterations, including cytoplasmic vacuolization and pyknotic, eccentrically displaced nuclei. Immunohistochemical staining confirmed extensive viral antigen expression across cortical layers IV and V, hippocampal pyramidal neurons, the stratum radiatum of the CA1 region, and local microglial extensions. Detailed immunohistochemical characterization of the neoplastic mass resolved phenotypic markers across distinct cell populations. The abundant histiocytic cells demonstrated intense cytoplasmic immunoreactivity for ionized calcium-binding adapter molecule 1 (Iba-1), predominantly organized at the outer margins of the tumor. Conversely, the central mononuclear lymphocytic cells lacked expression of the B-cell lineage marker PAX5 and the T-cell marker CD3, while CD3-positive T lymphocytes were restricted to perivascular cuffs in the adjacent neuroparenchyma. Furthermore, the tumor cells showed negative or negligible labeling for interferon regulatory factor 4 (IRF-4), excluding plasma cell neoplasia such as plasmacytoma or multiple myeloma. The lack of PAX5 expression ruled out a conventional diagnosis of histiocyte-rich B-cell lymphoma and led the investigators to hypothesize that the lesion represented a lymphoma undergoing transdifferentiation into a histiocytic or dendritic cell neoplasm. PAX5 is essential for maintaining B-cell identity, and its downregulation permits lymphoid progenitors to differentiate along macrophage and histiocytic lineages, as observed in histiocytic sarcomas. SARS-CoV-2 viral antigens were detected within the cytoplasm of neoplastic histiocytes located near infected neurons, potentially mediated by non-ACE2 entry pathways such as CD169. Due to the rapid seven-day timeline between inoculation and necropsy, the authors concluded that direct viral oncogenesis was unlikely, suggesting the mass arose spontaneously or advanced under acute viral-induced inflammation. To ensure diagnostic precision across the immunohistochemical evaluations, the investigators implemented rigorous procedural controls. Tissue sections prepared from a healthy mouse spleen served as positive reference standards for PAX5, CD3, and Iba-1 reactivity, whereas splenic tissue obtained from a mouse inoculated with myeloma cells provided a verified positive control for IRF-4 labeling. For negative controls, primary antibodies were systematically replaced with tris-buffered saline. Beyond identifying the mass itself, microscopic examination of the diencephalic region identified subtle structural alterations in the surrounding brain architecture. The positioning of the encapsulated nodule corresponded to the abrupt margin of the surviving cortical layer, suggesting that localized tissue atrophy had produced a loss of the lateroventral cortex directly adjacent to the lesion. The detection of viral antigen inside neoplastic histiocytes underscores questions regarding atypical viral entry mechanisms. Although SARS-CoV-2 neuroinvasion is predominantly facilitated by ACE2 expression, the researchers noted that the pathogen can penetrate histiocytes through type I lectin receptors, specifically CD169, without relying on ACE2 binding. This observed cellular tropism parallels earlier laboratory studies involving malignant cell cultures, which demonstrated active SARS-CoV-2 internalization in glioblastoma, hepatoma, and brain-metastatic lung cancer cell lines. In those experimental environments, infected cancer cells have been hypothesized to act as operational viral reservoirs that might facilitate viral dissemination during metastatic spread while directly affecting tumor progression and host survival. The authors also reviewed systemic immunological and molecular pathways that could link viral infection to lymphoid transformation. An established immunological concept involves an imbalance between T helper 1 and T helper 2 lymphocytes, which skews the immune response toward antibody-dependent pathways and correlates with elevated COVID-19 mortality. Molecularly, SARS-CoV-2 infection can upregulate microRNA miR-155, disrupting cellular regulation and promoting ongoing inflammatory cytokine signaling that stimulates B-cell proliferation. Additionally, the virus shares functional characteristics with oncogenic viruses such as Epstein-Barr virus and hepatitis B virus, which disrupt cellular defenses by promoting degradation of the tumor suppressor protein p53. Documented reductions in p53 levels among both acute and long COVID-19 patients further indicate a possible mechanism for elevated carcinogenic vulnerability. Microenvironmental stresses triggered by severe inflammatory cascades represent another contributing avenue under evaluation. Cellular responses to damage-associated molecular patterns and pathogen-associated molecular patterns generate localized tissue hypoxia. This hypoxic microenvironment stimulates the synthesis of lysyl oxidase, an enzyme that facilitates the migration and tissue invasion of neoplastic cells. Furthermore, isolated clinical reports have identified occurrences of B-cell and T-cell lymphomas following COVID-19 vaccination, where persistent lymphoid activation and chronic inflammation were implicated in malignant transformation. Although these vaccine-associated events remain rare, the authors posited that natural viral infection might produce comparable or more pronounced immune stimulation capable of influencing lymphoid stability in vulnerable subjects. The researchers emphasized notable experimental limitations that constrain definitive causal conclusions from this single case. The small overall dimensions and incipient developmental stage of the tumor restricted the availability of serial tissue sections, which prevented a more exhaustive diagnostic panel of immunohistochemical markers. In addition, the k18-hACE2 model carries inherent limitations due to the transgenic overexpression of human ACE2 under the cytokeratin 18 promoter, which induces unusually severe neuropathology and an exaggerated neuroinflammatory response upon viral challenge. Given the brief seven-day experimental duration and the rapid proliferation rate characteristic of murine tissues, the investigators could not exclude the possibility that the neoplasm developed spontaneously or arose through unrelated physiological factors rather than viral induction. supplementary_news.content: Abstract Post-severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2, COVID-19) interstitial lung disease (ILD) encompasses a heterogeneous spectrum of pulmonary abnormalities, ranging from resolving inflammatory changes to persistent fibrosis. Although most post-infectious abnormalities stabilize or regress over time, a subset of patients develop progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF). Distinguishing post-infectious sequelae from newly emerging or previously unrecognized PPF is a diagnostic challenge. We present two cases of PPF following severe COVID-19 pneumonia. The first patient, a 57-year-old man, developed persistent hypoxemic respiratory failure following COVID-19 infection in 2020. After several years of radiological stability, following a new-onset pneumonia, progressive restrictive lung disease developed, marked by fibrotic abnormalities on high-resolution computed tomography of the chest (HRCT). Despite corticosteroid and mycophenolate mofetil therapy, the patient continued to deteriorate, with the development of PPF. The second patient is a 64-year-old man who presented with predominantly ground-glass lung opacities and restrictive lung disease following severe COVID-19 pneumonia in 2021. Initial corticosteroid treatment resulted in substantial radiological improvement and subsequent stability. However, in 2025, new fibrotic changes, including subpleural honeycombing, emerged with significant physiological deterioration. In both patients, the diagnostic evaluation was limited by the absence of conclusive histopathological findings, but because of radiological and clinical progression, antifibrotic medication nintedanib was initiated, and the patients were referred for lung transplant evaluation. Our cases illustrate the heterogeneous and potentially progressive nature of pulmonary abnormalities following severe COVID-19 infection. PPF may develop several years after severe COVID-19 pneumonia, even with initial radiological improvement or prolonged stability. Because of the unpredictable course of the disease, the authors recommend continued evaluation with lung function testing and serial HRCT. For patients who progress despite medical therapy, early referral for lung transplant evaluation is advised. Introduction The severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2, COVID-19) pandemic resulted in health emergencies for millions worldwide. While many have recovered, the chronic sequelae of the disease continue to impact patients' lives. This is probably most apparent in those who survived severe COVID-19 pneumonia but develop interstitial lung disease (ILD), which often results in chronic disability. Little is known about the origin of post-COVID-19 ILD, but preliminary research based on lung pathology [1] distinguishes four types of interstitial lung changes: diffuse alveolar damage (DAD), organizing pneumonia (OP), nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP), and usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP). While these entities were initially recognized on lung pathology, they are now commonly used in the clinical description of the disease based on imaging [2]. DAD and OP usually represent inflammatory changes early in the course of the disease, and fibrosis associated with NSIP or UIP may form later. However, the temporal and etiological relationship of these entities remains unknown. Progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF) is defined as clinical, physiological, and radiological progression of already established pulmonary fibrosis. Patients must meet at least two of three criteria in the past one year: 1) worsening respiratory symptoms; 2) a change in pulmonary function test (PFT) marked by more than 5% decline in forced vital capacity (FVC) absolute value and/or more than 10% reduction in diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (DLCO) absolute value; 3) radiological progression in the extent or severity of bronchiectasis, formation of new ground-glass opacity (GGO) or reticulation, new or worsening honeycombing, or increase in lobar volume loss [3]. The purpose of this article is to present the diagnostic complexities of post-COVID-19 ILD and to provide a practical approach for these patients. Case Presentation Case 1 A 57-year-old gentleman with a medical history of multiple transient ischemic attacks (TIAs), previous cardiac surgery for atrial myxoma, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity, and a 22-pack-year smoking history developed severe COVID-19 pneumonia in April 2020. The disease course is shown in Figure 1. His occupational history was notable for asbestos exposure from work as a plumber, and he reported keeping two dogs at home. Although invasive ventilatory support was not required during the acute infection, he developed persistent hypoxemia requiring long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT). Initial PFT in October 2023 demonstrated restrictive ventilatory impairment marked by low FVC, low forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1), and severe reduction in DLCO. Post-hospitalization chest high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) showed mild and stable post-inflammatory reticulation in 2024. In March 2025, he developed pneumonia, which was treated with antibiotics and systemic corticosteroids as an outpatient. Following this episode, his preexisting hypoxemia worsened, and he was seen in our ILD clinic. HRCT of the chest demonstrated progressive lung disease with extensive fibrotic interstitial abnormalities without a particular pattern but primarily affecting the lower lobes. Neither traction bronchiectasis nor honeycombing was identified. A stable 9 mm pulmonary nodule was also present in the right upper lobe. Representative CT images are shown in Figure 2. Given the patient's medical, occupational, and exposure history, post-inflammatory lung fibrosis, asbestosis, GERD-associated microaspiration, primary lung cancer, systemic autoimmune rheumatic disease-associated interstitial lung disease (SARD-ILD), and chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis (CHP) were initially considered for the differential diagnosis of ILD. The differential diagnosis of ILD for Case 1 is shown in Table 1. Laboratory evaluation revealed only a low-titer positive antinuclear antibody (ANA; 1:40), while the remainder of the immunological work-up was unremarkable, suggesting against the presence of SARD-ILD. Both erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) levels were within the normal range. PFT demonstrated progressive, severe restrictive disease. During the six-minute walk test (6MWT), exercise capacity was impaired, and the patient was able to walk only 60 meters despite continuous supplemental oxygen. To evaluate the right upper lobe nodule and the ILD, endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS)-guided transbronchial needle aspiration, core biopsy, and transbronchial cryobiopsy were performed. Lung tissue was obtained from the right upper and left lower lobes, and the mediastinal lymph nodes were also sampled. Histopathological and cytological examinations revealed no evidence of malignancy, excluded histological changes associated with asbestos-related lung disease, aspiration, and CHP, but did not provide an alternative diagnosis of the origin of the ILD. The bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was neutrophil-predominant without infectious agents. Systemic corticosteroid therapy in combination with mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) was initiated in December 2025. Despite immunosuppressive treatment and completion of a pulmonary rehabilitation program, the patient's clinical condition continued to deteriorate, and his PFT declined in March 2026. HRCT of the chest in April 2026 demonstrated further radiological progression with early honeycombing. In view of the progressive fibrotic phenotype, antifibrotic therapy with nintedanib was started in April 2026. Cardiovascular assessment with stress echocardiography demonstrated preserved left ventricular function without evidence of clinically significant cardiac dysfunction contributing to his functional limitation. At the same time, optimization of glycemic control with semaglutide was associated with a 5 kg reduction in body weight. The patient met criteria for PPF because of a reduction in exercise tolerance marked by increasing LTOT, decline in FVC, and worsening pulmonary fibrosis with new honeycombing on imaging. Given the progressive nature of the pulmonary fibrosis and the increasing home oxygen need up to 6 L/min by June 2026, the patient was referred for lung transplant evaluation. Case 2 A 64-year-old never-smoker gentleman was evaluated in the ILD clinic. He had a complex medical history including Hodgkin lymphoma diagnosed in 1999, treated with chemotherapy and radiotherapy; hypothyroidism diagnosed in 2003; and a traumatic right-sided hydrothorax in 2007. In 2019, he developed diverticular disease requiring colostomy. His postoperative course was complicated by peritonitis necessitating reoperation in 2020, an incisional hernia with mesh repair, and another surgical intervention because of mesh-associated infection in October 2021. In December 2021, the patient developed severe COVID-19 pneumonia. Following recovery from the acute infection, LTOT was prescribed because of recurrent episodes of hypoxemia. Follow-up chest HRCT demonstrated multifocal, upper-lobe-predominant GGOs without traction bronchiectasis, accompanied by subpleural architectural distortion, reticulation, and air trapping. PFT demonstrated a moderate restrictive ventilatory defect and a moderate reduction in DLCO. The disease course for Case 2 is shown in Figure 3. Because of concomitant small-airway disease, inhaled corticosteroid/long-acting β2-agonist (ICS/LABA) therapy was initiated. In March 2022, the patient additionally received prednisone at a dose of 0.5 mg/kg/day for one month, followed by gradual tapering. A subsequent chest HRCT in May 2022 showed substantial regression of the GGO, with only mild residual post-inflammatory scarring. After three years of disease stability, in April 2025, the patient underwent coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) and synchronized electrical cardioversion for atrial fibrillation. Amiodarone was subsequently initiated for rhythm control. Following completion of cardiopulmonary rehabilitation, his cardiac function remained normal. However, there was a decline in lung function in May 2025. Amiodarone was stopped due to concerns for medication-induced ILD, but there was no evidence of radiological progression on repeat imaging. Initially, we considered amiodarone-induced pulmonary toxicity, chemotherapy-induced ILD, and radiation-induced lung injury for this patient, but because there was no temporal association between the exposures and ILD progression, these possibilities were excluded. The differential diagnosis for Case 2 is shown in Table 2. Immunological laboratory investigations were also initiated to rule out a developing SARD-ILD, but immune serologies were within the normal range. By August 2026, chest CT demonstrated newly developed, early subpleural honeycombing in multiple lobes. In view of the newly developed fibrotic changes, lung biopsy was offered to further evaluate the etiology of lung fibrosis. The patient declined the biopsy and preferred initiation of treatment. Following shared decision-making, antifibrotic therapy with nintedanib was started in August 2026. The patient met criteria for PPF because of the decline in FVC and DLCO, and worsening pulmonary fibrosis with new honeycombing was noted on HRCT. Referral was made for lung transplant evaluation. Representative CT images are shown in Figure 4. Discussion Post-COVID-19 ILD is currently a broad term that encompasses any interstitial abnormality following a COVID-19 infection. Based on the results of several population-based studies, the risk of developing ILD as a result of a COVID-19 infection increases by 3.6 to 11 times, although the accuracy of the data is based on diagnostic codes [4,5]. In the absence of additional test results (PFT, laboratory and histological findings), the accuracy of these data and the subtype of the resulting post-COVID-19 ILD cannot be determined. Currently, the most significant risk factor for fibrotic post-COVID-19 ILD is the severe disease course, especially the presence of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) [6], but age, male gender, and a history of smoking may contribute to the development of the disease [7]. During follow-up HRCT examinations, the presence of reticulations, traction bronchiectasis, and honeycombing may indicate the presence of fibrosis and, consequently, the development of ILD. While GGOs develop within a few weeks as a result of inflammatory processes and typically show regression over the course of months, fibrotic changes appear later and generally remain stagnant [8]. Respiratory symptoms and a decreased diffusion capacity are more likely to occur in conjunction with persistent pulmonary abnormalities [8]. The link between immunological diseases and post-COVID-19 conditions has been the focus of research for years. Based on the available data, COVID-19 infection may increase the risk of various autoimmune diseases [9,10]. However, the relationship between autoimmune diseases and post-COVID-19 ILD has yet to be fully elucidated. The reports on newly diagnosed cases of SARD-ILD following COVID-19 infection are purely observational. These case reports describe SARD-ILD following COVID-19 infection that was associated with rheumatoid arthritis, systemic sclerosis, myositis, or mixed connective tissue disease [11-14]. In the reviewed literature, lung biopsies were either not performed, or the biopsy did not contribute to the diagnosis, which makes it difficult to find an etiological relationship between COVID-19 infection and ILD. The International Multisociety Consensus Statement, published in 2025, provides recommendations for managing post-COVID-19 CT abnormalities based on the available scientific data [15]. According to the consensus, a thin-slice HRCT scan is recommended 3-6 months after a moderate-to-severe COVID-19 infection, and the frequency of follow-up could be determined based on the clinical picture in accordance with the "as low as reasonably achievable" (ALARA) principle [15]. In a prospective cohort study, Hernandez-Argudo et al. found that persistent lung radiographic abnormalities on HRCT one year after COVID-19 pneumonia increased the risk of persistent lung fibrosis [16]. In their study, NSIP and OP were the most common imaging findings, but DAD, which is a presentation of ongoing ARDS, was also frequent. However, UIP, which is associated with PPF, was not common [16]. In contrast, Konopka et al. reported that nine of 18 lung biopsies performed 2-12 months post COVID-19 infection showed UIP pattern fibrosis [1]. The discrepancies between the radiographic and pathological findings are most likely the result of differences in the timing of sampling and also the distribution of ILD, which is not homogeneous in the lung. To overcome some of these diagnostic challenges, current guidelines do not recommend lung biopsy in patients with a typical UIP as it will not change the therapeutic approach [3]. In cases without a typical UIP on imaging, a lung biopsy can be useful, but its availability is often limited by the patient’s poor functional status. Table 3 shows the common pathological and imaging findings in post-COVID-19 ILD. The treatment of PPF post-COVID-19 is also challenging. In the absence of clinical guidelines, the general approach follows the wisdom of non-COVID-19 ILD [17]. In primarily inflammatory disease, usually determined by more than 10% of GGO per lung surface on HRCT [3], we use immunosuppressive agents, including MMF, to prevent progression to fibrotic disease. In patients with primarily fibrotic disease with less than 10% of GGO on lung surface imaging, antifibrotic medication is preferred. Antifibrotic medications have been studied in progressive post-COVID-19 lung fibrosis, including pirfenidone and nintedanib, but these did not show any significant improvement in outcomes [18,19]. However, these studies were criticized for their broad inclusion criteria. In the case of patients with progressive NSIP, the current guideline provides only conditional recommendations for treatment [18] because the initial radiological findings do not necessarily correspond with disease progression. Identifying subgroups that show potential for progression may help to pinpoint target populations in which antifibrotics can improve clinical outcomes. While there are no guidelines on how to monitor patients with post-COVID-19 ILD, in our practice, we follow them similarly to those with non-COVID-19 ILD. PFT and 6MWT are performed every three to six months to monitor for stability, and a chest HRCT is recommended if lung function declines. We would like to emphasize that taking care of patients with ILD requires a multidisciplinary approach due to their multiple comorbidities. This usually includes primary care physicians, physical therapy, radiology, rheumatology, cardiology, and pulmonology. In cases with continued functional decline or a need for new home oxygen support despite medical therapy, early referral for lung transplant evaluation is recommended. Conclusions Post-COVID lung abnormalities mostly stabilize over time. However, in a small proportion of cases, progression and pulmonary fibrosis occur, accompanied by a decline in lung function and quality of life. Patients with progressive disease need close multidisciplinary monitoring. Our case series is limited by its purely descriptive nature, which does not allow broader interpretation. While we cannot draw long-term conclusions from our study, further investigations are needed to determine which subgroup of post-COVID-19 patients are at risk of progression and require early intervention. Researchers investigated how epidemiologically emerging viral strains interact with human peripheral blood mononuclear cells, tracing changes across antiviral, inflammatory, and antigen-presenting functions using high-dimensional immunophenotyping, secretome profiling, and functional assays. The investigation utilized a human peripheral blood mononuclear cell in vitro model to assess cellular reprogramming across multiple viral lineages. Investigators exposed primary immune cells to the ancestral D614G strain, alongside the Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta, Omicron BA.1, and recombinant Omicron XBB.1 variants, systematically comparing the immune signaling and cellular remodeling triggered by each lineage. Discover more Read Med Journals Get Health Tips Check Symptoms Single-cell multi-omic profiling following exposure to Omicron BA.1 revealed substantial remodeling across the innate immune compartment. The analysis identified a particularly marked dampening of monocyte differentiation and functional maturation, establishing circulating monocytes as primary targets for innate immune alteration following viral challenge. Discover more Study Anatomy Study Biology Get Rapid Tests Find Lung Care Direct tracking of viral components confirmed that the virus preferentially accumulated within monocytes. By conducting viral RNA mapping and detecting double-stranded RNA-positive cells, the study authors observed localized accumulation of viral material that directly coincided with transcriptomic reprogramming inside the monocyte population. Analysis of cytokine and chemokine production indicated that the emergence of Omicron altered the inflammatory baseline compared to earlier lineages. Omicron exposure produced a more balanced inflammatory profile characterized by preserved antiviral type I interferon responses and moderated chemokine induction, pointing toward a regulated virus-host equilibrium. The study demonstrated that this shifted equilibrium was associated with reduced innate immune-mediated tissue damage in vitro. While earlier lineages triggered distinct inflammatory patterns, the moderation of chemokine induction under Omicron exposure indicated variant-specific calibration of early host immune responses. In contrast to BA.1, the post-Omicron recombinant subvariant XBB.1 robustly re-engaged host antiviral pathways. Cellular stimulation with XBB.1 induced high type I interferon release and uniquely promoted interleukin-12p70 production, highlighting divergence among closely related Omicron sublineages. The induction of interleukin-12p70 by XBB.1 drove the expansion of specific dendritic cell populations, including antiviral, mature PD-L1-positive CD80-positive plasmacytoid dendritic cells and BDCA3-positive conventional dendritic cells. These expanded dendritic cell subsets directly supported the priming of CD8-positive T cells. The authors concluded that circulating variants possess intrinsic differences that govern monocyte targeting, inflammation, and antigen presentation. These observations provide a detailed laboratory framework for evaluating how progressive viral mutations influence innate immune defense and subsequent cellular interactions in vitro. Developed from the monoclonal antibody ADG20, or adintrevimab, VYD222 exhibits substantially improved potency and breadth across an array of emerging viral lineages despite extensive mutations in the viral spike protein that inactivated earlier therapeutic antibodies. VYD222 previously received Emergency Use Authorization from the United States Food and Drug Administration for pre-exposure prophylaxis of COVID-19 in selected immunocompromised adult and adolescent populations. In laboratory evaluations, researchers confirmed that the antibody maintains potent neutralization across a broad panel of emergent variants, including the recently dominant XFG lineage. X-ray crystal structures of VYD222 bound to the receptor-binding domains of both prototype SARS-CoV-2 and the Omicron BA.5 variant reveal the molecular mechanisms underlying its activity. These structural complexes illustrate how VYD222 accommodates specific spike mutations that previously allowed viral variants to evade earlier authorized monoclonal antibodies. Discover more Study Biology Get Rapid Tests Order DNA Kits Track Biotech Find Lung Care Structural evaluations show that multiple engineered mutations separating VYD222 from its parental antibody ADG20 occur in the second shell outside direct paratope contact residues. Deep mutational scanning further demonstrates that viral escape from VYD222 is constrained by structural compatibility requirements and the virus’s necessity to maintain host receptor binding. These structural and functional findings elucidate the escape-resistant neutralization properties of VYD222 against clinically relevant SARS-CoV-2 variants. The authors note that the mechanistic insights offer guidance for assessing risk associated with emerging viral lineages. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Monday, November 23, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Captive Wildlife in South Africa Faces Ongoing SARS-CoV-2 Reverse Zoonosis Risks by November 18, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Captive Wildlife in South Africa Faces Ongoing SARS-CoV-2 Reverse Zoonosis Risks Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A multi-year One Health investigation conducted across four provinces in South Africa has revealed continued risks of reverse zoonotic SARS-CoV-2 transmission from humans to captive and free-ranging wildlife. Researchers monitoring susceptible animal populations between 2021 and 2025 confirmed active viral infections and serological evidence of exposure in multiple captive carnivore species. The study evaluated a cohort of 92 animals situated across Gauteng, Limpopo, Western Cape, and Mpumalanga Provinces. Animals were selected for investigation based on the presentation of clinical respiratory signs, unexplained mortality, or opportunistic sampling among species recognized as having high susceptibility to coronavirus infection. Investigators collected respiratory specimens to detect viral ribonucleic acid and obtained serum samples to evaluate immunoglobulin G antibody responses against SARS-CoV-2. In addition to testing for SARS-CoV-2, the team comprehensively screened respiratory samples for other potential infectious agents, including alternative coronaviruses, influenza A virus, and paramyxoviruses, ensuring that co-infections or secondary respiratory pathogens were thoroughly characterized. Molecular diagnostic testing using reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction detected SARS-CoV-2 RNA in four of the 92 tested animals, representing an overall detection rate of 4.3 percent. These confirmed cases comprised three lions sampled in Gauteng Province during 2021 and an exotic jaguar housed at a private zoological facility in Limpopo Province during 2023. Notably, the infected jaguar developed severe systemic and respiratory pathology that ultimately resulted in the animal’s death, highlighting the lethal vulnerability of certain exotic felids to coronavirus exposure in managed captive settings. Discover more Check Symptoms Read Med Journals Get Rapid Tests Find Lung Care Book a Safari Beyond molecular detection of active shedding, serological screening indicated that viral exposure was substantially more widespread across captive populations than identified by polymerase chain reaction alone. Serological tests performed on 45 animals identified SARS-CoV-2 immunoglobulin G antibodies in six individuals, establishing a seropositivity rate of 13.3 percent. The seropositive animals included three lions, one lynx, one puma, and one mongoose. While the lynx and puma remained entirely asymptomatic and were housed at the same zoological facility as the three infected lions, the seropositive mongoose exhibited overt respiratory symptoms following close human contact at a wildlife reserve in Mpumalanga Province. To investigate the transmission chain and potential human sources of infection, the research team instituted contact tracing among facility personnel. Screening of zoo employees and veterinary staff who had potential contact with the affected animals identified one veterinary student who tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 RNA via reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction. Partial genomic sequencing and phylogenetic analysis performed on viral RNA recovered from the fatal jaguar case classified the pathogen as Omicron sublineage BA.2. The researchers concluded that captive wildlife and free-ranging species in close proximity to human handlers or visitors face an enduring threat of reverse zoonosis post-pandemic. The fatal progression observed in the exotic jaguar emphasizes the critical need for continued vigilance at human-animal interfaces. The authors emphasize that sustained, integrated One Health genomic and serological surveillance remains indispensable for detecting novel viral spillovers, tracking lineage diversifications across host species, and mitigating transmission hazards among vulnerable wildlife populations. supplementary_news.content_title: University students were the first to spread new SARS-CoV-2 variants — Nature
supplementary_news.content: News Around the World University students were the first to spread new SARS-CoV-2 variants — Nature Fedir Kryshtovskyi 19 November 2026 20:44 In Massachusetts, an analysis of more than 85,000 SARS-CoV-2 genome sequences showed that university students consistently began spreading new genetic variants of the virus first. The highest level of COVID-19 transmission in 2021–2023 was also recorded among school students aged 15–18 and residents of elderly care facilities. Testing data in Massachusetts As Nature reports, researchers combined genomic data with epidemiological information about people with COVID-19, including their age and vaccination status. They used test results collected in Massachusetts from November 2021 to January 2023. Genome sequencing made it possible to track the spread of SARS-CoV-2 variants that emerged during this period. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram . Risks for workers At the same time, employees of schools, universities and elderly care facilities had approximately the same risk of contracting COVID-19 as people in the communities surrounding these institutions. The authors of the analysis also found that booster vaccinations reduced the transmission of SARS-CoV-2, including the Omicron BA.1 variant, which began circulating in Massachusetts in late 2021. The study results were published on November 19, 2026, in the journal Cell. Epidemiologist Bill Hanage of the Harvard School of Public Health called the scale of the work an impressive example of the capabilities of population genomics. Read us on Download our app

supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Monday, November 23, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Lower Neutralizing Antibodies Correlate With Protracted Illness in Longitudinal COVID-19 Study by November 21, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Lower Neutralizing Antibodies Correlate With Protracted Illness in Longitudinal COVID-19 Study Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A longitudinal study analyzing serum samples from COVID-19 patients at UCLA-affiliated hospitals has revealed significant correlations between host neutralizing antibody levels, clinical disease trajectories, and the ongoing evolutionary adaptations of SARS-CoV-2 variants. Researchers evaluated the neutralizing capacity of antibodies targeting the viral spike protein receptor-binding domain to track how humoral immunity interacts with viral mutation and patient outcomes across distinct pandemic waves. The investigation examined 305 longitudinal serum samples collected from 86 patients infected during the initial pre-vaccine wave, alongside cohorts of 20 individuals during the Omicron period and 18 individuals during the post-Omicron period. By deploying virus neutralization tests against the SARS-CoV-2 receptor-binding domain, the authors quantified neutralizing antibody inhibition scores across patient populations over extended timelines following confirmed infection. Discover more Book Care Services Find Therapists Get Health Tips Among the 86 first-wave patients, researchers evaluated 300 serum samples collected at various time points after infection and stratified antibody responses into percentile-based groups based on inhibition scores ranging from 1 to 100. The lower 25th percentile cohort, designated S25, comprised 29 patients who consistently exhibited low neutralization scores below 25, registering a median score of 7.46 with a 95 percent confidence interval from 6.1 to 8.8. Discover more Study Biology Track Biotech Check Symptoms COVID-19 The middle 50th percentile group, labeled S50, included 44 patients with intermediate neutralizing antibody scores falling between 25 and 75, exhibiting a median score of 45.77 and a 95 percent confidence interval from 39.5 to 52.1. The upper 75th percentile group, designated S75, consisted of 13 patients displaying consistently elevated neutralization scores above 75, with a median score of 88 and a 95 percent confidence interval from 75.95 to 85.52. Temporal analysis of humoral immunity demonstrated that peak neutralizing antibody activity occurred at a median of approximately 18 days following SARS-CoV-2 infection. Neutralization activity remained detectable in longitudinal patient sera past 100 days post-infection, establishing a clear baseline for tracking how antibody persistence correlates with long-term viral clearance and clinical progression. Hospital records revealed marked differences in healthcare utilization and symptom duration corresponding to these neutralizing antibody tiers. Patients in the low-antibody S25 group experienced a median of two hospital visits or admissions compared to a median of one visit among S75 patients. Furthermore, S25 patients had significantly longer hospitalizations with persistent COVID-19 symptoms, recording a median stay of 41 days compared to 31 days for the S75 group. Reflecting the need for prolonged clinical monitoring, patients in the S25 tier underwent a greater total number of diagnostic PCR tests throughout their hospital courses. Analysis of therapeutic interventions indicated that S25 individuals primarily received medications such as remdesivir or corticosteroids between days 60 and 200, whereas the S50 cohort received treatments predominantly within the first 50 days and the S75 cohort within the initial 30 days. Discover more Get Rapid Tests Read Med Journals Read Health News Find Treatments Find Lung Care Clinical manifestations also diverged markedly between cohorts, as patients with low neutralizing antibody titers suffered protracted illness without acute respiratory collapse. Conversely, individuals in the S50 and S75 groups required immediate pharmaceutical and respiratory intervention and displayed greater vulnerability to acute respiratory distress syndrome during early hospitalization. Underlying comorbidities showed distinct distributions across antibody tiers that may explain divergent immune responses. A substantial proportion of patients in the high-antibody S75 group presented with hypertension, whereas the low-antibody S25 group contained individuals with immunosuppressive conditions such as solid organ transplantation and active chemotherapy, factors that likely attenuated early humoral responses and delayed viral clearance. Testing serum efficacy across viral lineages demonstrated a pronounced reduction in neutralization capacity against newer SARS-CoV-2 variants relative to the ancestral wild-type strain. First-wave patient sera exhibited steep declines in neutralizing activity against BA.1, BA.5, BQ.1.1, XBB, and XBB.1.5, with post-Omicron sera maintaining comparatively higher overall neutralization titers likely resulting from updated vaccinations or hybrid immunity. Comparative binding assays focusing on the XBB sublineage highlighted the biochemical mechanisms driving variant dominance, identifying the solitary S486P amino acid substitution in the receptor-binding domain of XBB.1.5. While neutralization levels against XBB.1 and XBB.1.5 remained comparable in patient sera, optical density measurements confirmed that XBB.1.5 achieved markedly higher binding affinity to the human ACE2 receptor. The authors noted important methodological limitations, emphasizing that the investigation was conducted as a single-center retrospective study with imbalanced cohort sizes across the first wave, Omicron, and post-Omicron periods. Incomplete vaccination and infection records further constrained causal interpretations, leading the research team to call for multi-center longitudinal evaluations to corroborate these immunological and clinical observations. The epidemiological findings contextualize the global impact of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 following its initial identification in Wuhan, China, in December 2019. By December 2024, global records confirmed over 800 million cases and more than 7.1 million deaths worldwide. Although immunization had reached over 70 percent of the global population with at least one vaccine dose by late 2024, contributing to rising seroprevalence and declining daily infections across many regions, emerging variants continue to challenge containment. Waning antibody immunity and the emergence of lineages with greater transmissibility and immune evasion have necessitated booster immunizations alongside ongoing public health surveillance. At the structural level, viral entry into human host cells is mediated by the spike protein, which binds directly to the human angiotensin converting enzyme 2 receptor. Highly mutable regions within this surface protein dictate infection severity and drive immune evasion. Human antibodies directed against receptor-specific epitopes on the spike protein serve as the established correlate of protection against COVID-19 infection. Within the spike protein, the receptor binding domain represents the primary target for neutralizing antibodies. Because neutralizing antibody titers vary widely across individuals, virus neutralization tests established early in the pandemic provide quantitative measurements that offer direct predictive value for evaluating protection against infection. Throughout the pandemic, selective pressures within the spike protein have generated successive variants of concern, including the Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta, and Omicron lineages. Emerging subvariants have acquired key mutations that enhance viral fitness and render historical antibody titers progressively ineffective. This evolutionary progression is exemplified by the JN.1 variant, a sublineage derived from BA.2.86 that accumulated notable spike substitutions including L452W and N481K. These mutations conferred heightened transmissibility and immune escape, demonstrating how continuous structural adaptations challenge host defenses and require updated neutralization tests and adapted vaccine compositions to maintain effective population protection. In laboratory evaluations of patient sera across pandemic periods, the authors identified marked differences in neutralization efficacy against specific viral variants. Sera from patients infected during the Omicron wave demonstrated robust neutralizing capacity against the ancestral wild-type strain, with most patient samples exceeding 60 percent neutralization efficacy. However, neutralizing activity against earlier Omicron lineages displayed notable variability. When tested against the BA.1 and BA.5 variants, patient sera exhibited divergent responses, ranging from high neutralization exceeding 90 percent efficacy in certain individuals to an undetectable level of neutralizing activity in others. This observation contrasted with previously published reports from independent cohorts. Although BA.5 possesses specific mutations in the receptor binding domain, namely L452R and F486V, that effectively evade antibodies elicited by vaccination or BA.1 infection, the UCLA cohort showed comparatively lower neutralization against BA.1 than against BA.5. The authors attributed this pattern to cohort demographics and historical public health timelines. In the United States, primary vaccination and booster campaigns occurred extensively throughout 2021, and the lifting of indoor mask mandates in early-to-mid 2022 resulted in widespread community exposure to BA.5, generating elevated antibody titers against that specific variant. Testing across later lineages indicated diminishing neutralization against BQ.1, XBB, and XBB.1.5, reflecting potential immune escape among newly emerging variants. In contrast, serum samples from the post-Omicron cohort consistently retained higher neutralization scores across tested variants compared to first-wave sera. This elevated neutralizing capacity demonstrates substantial improvement in humoral immunity over time, which the researchers linked to the combined immunological benefits of updated vaccination and natural exposure across successive pandemic waves. The investigation also clarified the biochemical mechanisms enabling XBB.1.5 to achieve dominance over its parental variant XBB.1. Genomic analysis identified a solitary amino acid substitution, S486P, in the receptor binding domain of XBB.1.5. Although neutralization titers between XBB.1 and XBB.1.5 were similar, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays revealed distinct receptor binding properties. Comparing optical density at 450 nanometers across log-transformed concentrations demonstrated that XBB.1.5 exhibited steeper sigmoidal curves and higher optical density readings at lower protein concentrations, confirming enhanced binding affinity for the human ACE2 receptor. This indicates that dominant SARS-CoV-2 variants emerge through combined pressures of antibody evasion and increased receptor affinity. Finally, the authors examined how host health conditions influenced antibody production and clinical progression. In the low-antibody S25 cohort, immunosuppressive conditions including organ transplantation and chemotherapy likely blunted initial humoral responses. The researchers suggested these comorbidities attenuated early acute inflammation while delaying viral clearance, explaining why S25 patients experienced protracted hospitalizations and persistent symptoms without severe acute manifestations, ultimately receiving medications between days 60 and 200. In contrast, patients with higher neutralizing antibody levels mounted vigorous early immune responses that triggered acute respiratory distress requiring prompt therapeutic intervention within the initial 30 to 50 days, illustrating how baseline host factors shape clinical trajectories. supplementary_news.content_title: Ruedas-Gracia, Tiwari Examine Effects of COVID-19 on Belonging
supplementary_news.content: Nidia Ruedas-Gracia, assistant professor Educational Psychology, and Ananya Tiwari, Ph.D. '23 EPSY, have co-written an article in the Journal of Research on Adolescence that examines the COVID-19 pandemic and it's effects on marginalized girls in India. The study, “Belonging in crisis: A mixed-methods exploration of school disruption among marginalized girls in India,” examines how prolonged COVID-19 school closures reshaped school belonging among marginalized adolescent girls in rural India. Using a bioecological and intersectional lens, it looks at how household labor, digital access, relationships with family, peers, and teachers, and broader gender, caste, and class inequities shaped girls’ connection to school. One key finding is that belonging became increasingly constrained the longer schools stayed closed. "I think it's a great example of the global reach of the work coming out of our doctoral program," says Ruedas-Gracia. "It offers timely lessons about supporting students' sense of belonging when schooling is disrupted." Read the full article here

settings 【字体: 大 中 小 】 时间:2026年11月21日 来源:Cell 45.1 编辑推荐: 理解呼吸道病毒传播需要将病原体基因组数据与详细的流行病学背景相结合。研究人员分析了 2021 年 11 月至 2023 年 1 月在美国马萨诸塞州收集的超过 85,000 例带有流行病学数据的 SARS-CoV-2 基因组(严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒 2,SA 欢迎领取《类器官应用方案 3D之旅》 为了促进科学的传播,生物通采集了这篇文章 订阅BioHot点这里解锁原文链接推送! “畅读会员”点此登录查看原文链接 Article Open access 理解呼吸道病毒传播需要将病原体基因组数据与详细的流行病学背景相结合。研究人员分析了 2021 年 11 月至 2023 年 1 月在美国马萨诸塞州收集的超过 85,000 例带有流行病学数据的 SARS-CoV-2 基因组(严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒 2,SARS-CoV-2)。这些数据来自 666 个场所,包括学校、大学和技术护理机构(skilled nursing facilities,SNFs),使得场所内传播与社区传播风险能够进行直接比较。传播升高集中存在于特定的年龄定义亚群中,包括学校中的高年级青少年、大学中的本科生以及护理机构中的居住者,而其他群体,尤其是工作人员,并未表现出额外风险。年轻成人,特别是大学生,在传播中发挥了不成比例的作用,新的病毒谱系也持续首先在该群体中扩增。病毒扩散呈现出可重复的城市向乡村梯度,疫苗接种与下游传播减少相关。研究人员进一步估计了及时检测新出现变异株所需的测序阈值。总体而言,这些发现揭示了 SARS-CoV-2 传播中一致的人口学和空间结构,可为呼吸道病毒病原体的基因组监测提供依据。 研究背景与意义 欢迎领取《全方位集成的高通量阵列式 SPR 平台》领 取 呼吸道病毒传播的驱动机制不能仅依靠病毒序列变化来解释,还需要把基因组数据与个体年龄、接种状态、居住地、检测场所等流行病学元数据结合起来。此前大规模基因组监测主要服务于新变异株的发现和追踪,虽然能够描绘谱系更替,却往往缺少足够的现场背景,难以回答传播究竟发生在哪些人群、哪些机构环境以及哪些地理通道中。尤其在疫情后期,学校、大学、技术护理机构(skilled nursing facilities,SNFs)和工作场所重新开放或维持运行后,场所内传播是否高于社区背景风险、工作人员是否承担额外风险、年轻成人是否推动新谱系早期扩张,都是公共卫生决策需要证据支持的问题。 这项研究基于马萨诸塞州大范围诊断检测和测序体系,把超过 85,000 例带流行病学元数据的 SARS-CoV-2 基因组与 666 个检测场所联系起来,覆盖 Delta(B.1.1.617.2*)晚期流行以及 BA.1*、BA.2*、BA.4*、BA.5*、BQ.1*、XBB* 等连续 Omicron 亚变体波次。其价值不在于单纯报告变异株比例,而在于用近端遗传相关性(genetic relatedness)作为传播链代理,比较同一场所内病毒基因组是否比同一市镇社区样本更接近,从而识别年龄、场所、城市和接种状态如何共同塑造传播结构。 主要技术方法概括 样本队列来源于 Broad Institute 临床实验室在马萨诸塞州开展的 SARS-CoV-2 诊断检测残余阳性样本,并结合马萨诸塞州公共卫生部及市政卫生部门收集的病例流行病学数据。研究对 134,785 条高质量基因组进行 Pango 谱系注释和 Nextclade 质控,核心分析使用其中 85,125 条带年龄、性别、居住地、接种状态和检测场所元数据的数据。方法上主要采用近端遗传相关性富集分析判断场所内传播是否高于社区背景,利用系统发育树推断州内外输入和市镇间扩散,通过逻辑回归比较不同场所、年龄组和城市类型中新谱系达到 50% 频率的时间差,借助宿主内单核苷酸变异(intrahost single nucleotide variants,iSNVs)识别潜在下游传播,并用二项模型和 PhyloSamp 评估不同每周测序量对新谱系检测时效的影响。 研究结果 超过 85,000 个 SARS-CoV-2 基因组与个体化流行病学数据配对 研究获得 2021 年 11 月 1 日至 2023 年 1 月 17 日期间马萨诸塞州居民的 134,785 条高质量 SARS-CoV-2 基因组,覆盖 492 个 Pango 谱系,并归并为 Delta(B.1.1.617.2*)以及 BA.1*、BA.2*、BA.4*、BA.5*、BQ.1*、XBB* 七个主导谱系。样本来自 666 个机构,分为公共检测、大学、医院诊所、技术护理机构、中小学、其他工作场所和未知部门等七类;其中 85,125 条基因组可链接到去标识化流行病学数据,构成下游分析核心数据集。测序样本总体跟随全州确诊病例趋势,研究期平均每周测序约 10.5% 的确诊病例,为跨场所和跨时间的传播比较提供了高密度基础。 不同人口群体呈现差异化传播模式 研究人员以“同一场所内相距 ≤2 个核苷酸替换且采样间隔 ≤10 天的近缘基因组”相对于同市镇公共检测样本的富集倍数,衡量场所内传播是否超过社区背景。结果显示,技术护理机构近缘基因组富集 4.9 倍(95% CI 4.3–5.5),大学富集 3.3 倍(95% CI 3.1–3.6),中小学仅 1.4 倍(95% CI 1.2–1.7),其他工作场所 1.1 倍(95% CI 0.9–1.3)且不显著。年龄分层进一步表明,风险升高并非机构本身普遍属性,而是集中在特定年龄组:技术护理机构中约 50 岁以后随年龄上升,最高龄者同场所近缘性高出社区约 60 个百分点;学校中主要出现在 15–18 岁,18 岁左右达峰,低龄学生和教职员工接近社区水平;大学中主要集中在 18–22 岁本科生,18–20 岁最强,研究生、教师和工作人员不明显。BA.1*、BA.2*、BA.2.12.1* 在大学达到 50% 频率的时间比其他部门早 4–13 天;排除无症状筛查偏倚后,大学仍最早出现谱系上升,支持年轻成人群体作为早期扩增哨兵人群。 高分辨率时空图谱刻画病毒扩散 研究利用市镇级居住信息和系统发育重建,识别州外输入与州内市镇间移动。新输入显著集中于人口规模大、密度高的城市,城市既是州外输入受体,也是州内扩散源。BA.1* 和 BA.2* 均先在波士顿核心区升高,随后扩散至成熟郊区、区域城市中心、发展中郊区和乡村城镇。遗传距离与地理距离关系显示,≤2 个替换的近缘病毒对主要位于约 15 公里内;当差异累积到 3–5 个替换,即约 4 代传播、约 20 天后,病毒对已可能相隔 100 公里以上;差异超过约 12 个替换时地理结构基本消失,对应约两个月内全州广泛扩散。乡村和发展中郊区同市镇近缘富集达 11.3 倍,高于城市区域的 5.6 倍,说明乡村本地传播链更封闭,而城市承担输入与再分配枢纽角色。 疫苗接种与感染和下传传播减少相关 研究利用 5–11 岁儿童接种推广前后的自然时间点比较发现,学校检测和公共检测中该年龄段病例占比均下降约 50%,Delta 与 BA.1* 均可见。传播层面用两类基因组代理指标评估:一是有无近缘基因组链接,二是宿主内单核苷酸变异(intrahost single nucleotide variants,iSNVs)是否在后继个体共识序列中出现。加强针接种者更常表现为“未链接”,比例为 33.2%,而未加强者为 19.1%;以 iSNVs 判定下游传播时,加强针个体启动至少一次传播的可能性为未接种者的 0.65 倍(0.50–0.84)。仅完成基础免疫而未加强者与未接种者差异不显著。Ct 值分析显示接种剂次增加与较低病毒载量相关,距末次接种时间延长与病毒载量轻度回升相关,但行为混杂不能被排除。 测序强度决定新谱系检测速度 基于全部 130,000 条基因组进行降采样模拟,研究发现每周测序 100 条基因组时,多数谱系能在其达到 1% 流行率前被检出;每周 50 条通常只延迟数天;检测概率随测序量上升到每周约 500 条后趋于平台期。BA.1* 因增长过快,提高测序量对提前发现帮助有限。若目标是识别“正在指数增长的新谱系”,从 3% 频率后开始拟合逻辑增长,每周 300 条可在 14 天内确认 BA.1* 类快速上升谱系;对 BA.5* 这类慢增长谱系,14 天内确认几乎不可达到,21 天内确认至少需每周 400 条。 讨论与研究结论翻译 讨论部分指出,在学校、大学和技术护理机构中,SARS-CoV-2 传播升高主要不是机构环境的普遍效应,而是由特定年龄亚群驱动;工作人员、低龄学生以及多数其他工作场所并未显示明显高于社区的传播风险。技术护理机构是唯一呈现稳定场所内传播富集的场景,风险主要指向老年居住者;学校和大学的风险集中在 15–18 岁及 18–22 岁,可能与该年龄段的社交网络和住宿模式有关。18–22 岁人群,尤其大学生,是新谱系早期扩增的前哨群体。空间上,新谱系优先经大城市输入,再向郊区、区域城市和乡村扩散,约两个月完成全州铺开;因此城市应侧重阻断输入,乡村应侧重切断本地传播链。测序监测方面,中等且持续的覆盖率已能获得大部分早期预警收益,过高测序量的边际增益有限。作者同时强调,数据来自机会性监测,缺少未感染者接种信息和个体行为数据,不能做因果推断。 研究结论部分可译为:大规模基因组监测加深了对 COVID-19 大流行期间 SARS-CoV-2 变异株出现与扩散的认识,但缺乏详细元数据常限制更深入的流行病学分析。本研究利用跨多个变异株波次、高分辨率、并与流行病学元数据链接的大规模 SARS-CoV-2 基因组监测数据,考察了病毒传播的时空格局、不同人口群体和场所之间传播动力学的差异,以及与感染和下游传播相关的因素;同时给出了及时检测已知关注变异株、识别频率上升的未知变异株所需测序率的实用估计。尽管数据来自快速演变公共卫生应急中的机会式基因组监测,本研究仍展示了整合基因组与流行病学信息以解析精细尺度传播格局的能力。通过识别最可能在场所内外驱动传播的人群,以及新变异株最可能被检测到的时点,研究结果为未来基因组监测系统设计提供了可操作依据,尤其支持对高传播人群进行定向采样。
